The H-1B classification is also for aliens of distinguished merit and ability in the field of fashion modeling.
Write H-1B3 in the classification block.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or U.S. agent. The petitioner must submit evidence that establishes the
beneficiary will perform services at events or productions of a distinguished reputation. Such evidence includes:
1. Documentary evidence (such as certifications, affidavits, and reviews) to establish the beneficiary is a fashion model
of distinguished merit and ability. Any affidavits submitted by present or former employers or recognized experts
must set forth their expertise of the affiant and the manner in which the affiant acquired such information; and
2. Copies of any written contracts between the petitioner and the beneficiary or, if there is no written agreement, a
summary of the terms of the oral agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
General H-1B Requirements
Three relevant laws impacting the filing of H-1B and/or L visa petitions; include:
1. The American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA), Public Law 105-277 (signed into
law on October 21, 1998);
2. The H-1B Visa Reform Act of 2004 (signed into law on December 8, 2004); and
3. Public Law 114-113 (signed into law on December 18, 2005).
Because of ACWIA, H-1B and H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant petitioners must complete the H-1B Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, which is part of this petition. We use this supplement (formerly issued separately as
Form I-129W) to collect additional information about the H-1B nonimmigrant workers and the H-1B petitioners, and to
determine the applicability of fees mandated by ACWIA (INA section 214(c)(9)), the H-1B1 Visa Reform Act of 2004
(INA section 214(c)(12)), and Public Law 114-113.
A petitioner seeking initial approval of H-1B or L nonimmigrant status for a beneficiary, or seeking approval to employ an
H-1B or L nonimmigrant currently working for another employer, must submit an additional $500 Fraud Prevention and
Detection fee. This fee does not apply to H-1B1 petitions. The Form I-129 will serve as the vehicle for collection of the
$500 fee.
Those petitioners required to submit the $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee are also required to submit either an
additional $4,000 (H-1B) or $4,500 (L-1) fee mandated by Public Law 114-113, if:
1. The petitioner employs 50 or more individuals in the United States;
2. More than 50 percent of those employees are in H-1B or L-1A or L-1B nonimmigrant status; and
3. The petition is filed on or after December 18, 2015.
The Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee and Public Law 114-113 Fee, when applicable, may not be waived. Each
fee should be submitted by separate check or money order.
To determine if they are subject to any of these fees, petitioners must complete the H-1B and H1B1 Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement discussed below.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 10 of 30
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent who seek to place a beneficiary in H-1B classification (including H-1B1 classification for
free trade aliens from Chile and Singapore) must file this supplement.
The supplement is used to:
1. Collect additional information about the H-1B employer and beneficiary; and
2. Determine the appropriate American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA) fee. The ACWIA
Fee is a training fee meant to fund the training of U.S. workers. But if the employer has 25 or fewer full-time
employees, they must pay only one-half of the required fee at INA 214(c)(9)(B). This supplement also helps to
determine whether the beneficiary is subject to the H-1B numerical limitation (also known as the H-1B Cap). Please
note that the ACWIA fee may not be assessed to the beneficiary.
Who is required to submit this supplement?
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent seeking to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant worker
must file this supplement with the Form I-129 and the appropriate fee. (See What is the Filing Fee, for more information
about the appropriate fee.)
Completing Section 1. of the H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement Form
All petitioners who seek to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant worker must answer every
question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.

Great question — and yes, there are definitely tax implications to be aware of before you pull money from a retirement plan early.

**Quick note first:** I noticed you've been asking about tax deductions on salary and now early retirement withdrawals. If any of this relates to a specific financial situation you're working through, it may be worth running the numbers with a tax professional or CPA, since the details matter a lot.

**Here are the key tax implications of an early withdrawal (before age 59½):**

**1. Ordinary income tax**
Withdrawals from a traditional 401(k) or traditional IRA are taxed as ordinary income in the year you take them. That money gets added to your taxable income, which could push you into a higher tax bracket and potentially affect other things tied to income.

**2. The 10% early distribution penalty**
If you're under age 59½, you'll generally owe an additional 10% penalty on the amount withdrawn — on top of the income tax. So a $10,000 withdrawal could cost you, say, $2,200 in federal tax plus $1,000 in penalty, depending on your bracket.

**3. Exceptions to the penalty (but not always the income tax)**
There are some exceptions where the 10% penalty is waived, such as:
- Qualified birth or adoption expenses (up to $5,000)
- Certain medical expenses exceeding a percentage of your income
- First-time home purchase (up to $10,000, IRAs only)
- Qualified higher education expenses (IRAs only)
- Permanent disability or death
- A qualified disaster distribution

Even when the penalty is waived, you'll typically still owe income tax on the withdrawal.

**4. Roth accounts work differently**
With a Roth IRA or Roth 401(k), you've already paid tax on your contributions, so those come out tax-free. But earnings withdrawn early can be taxable and penalized. There's also a 5-year rule for Roth accounts to be aware of.

**5. Tax withholding**
Your plan administrator will typically withhold 20% for federal taxes on a 401(k) distribution. That doesn't necessarily cover your full tax bill — you could still owe more at filing time, or face an underpayment penalty.

**6. Impact beyond taxes**
It's also worth knowing that early withdrawals reduce your future retirement savings and you lose the tax-deferred growth on that money. Some plans also allow loans instead of withdrawals, which avoid taxes and penalties if repaid — worth checking whether that's an option for you.

If you tell me which type of account (401(k) vs. IRA, traditional vs. Roth) and roughly how old you are, I can help you think through the specifics more precisely. And again, a tax pro can model the exact impact for your bracket.

Yes — early withdrawals from a retirement plan generally come with significant tax consequences. Here's what to be aware of:

**1. Income tax on the withdrawal**
Any amount you withdraw from a traditional 401(k) or traditional IRA is added to your taxable income for the year. If it's a large withdrawal, it could push you into a higher tax bracket and potentially affect other things tied to your income (e.g., certain credits or Medicare premiums later on).

**2. 10% early withdrawal penalty**
If you're **under age 59½**, you'll typically owe an additional **10% penalty** on the amount withdrawn, on top of regular income tax. So a $10,000 withdrawal could cost you roughly $1,000 in penalty plus your marginal tax rate.

**3. Exceptions to the penalty**
There are cases where the 10% penalty is waived (income tax still applies), such as:
- Qualified birth or adoption expenses (up to $5,000)
- Certain medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of AGI
- Permanent disability
- Being a qualified reservist called to active duty
- Substantially equal periodic payments (SEPP/72(t))
- First-time homebuyer (up to $10,000, IRAs only)
- Qualified disaster distributions

Rules differ slightly between IRAs and 401(k)s, and some plans allow loans instead of withdrawals — worth checking.

**4. Roth accounts**
Roth contributions come out tax- and penalty-free, but **earnings** are taxed and penalized if withdrawn before 59½ and before the account is 5 years old.

**5. Employer plan specifics**
401(k)s often require you to meet certain conditions to withdraw while still employed, and some plans allow hardship withdrawals. Rollover to an IRA first may give you more options, but do the math on timing.

**A few things to check before you act:**
- Your exact age and plan type (401k vs. IRA, traditional vs. Roth)
- Whether a **loan** could meet your need without triggering taxes
- Whether you can wait until a lower-income year to withdraw

One quick note tied to your situation: since you're a private-sector firefighter, check whether your plan has special provisions — some public safety roles have different rules (though those more often apply to certain public/government plans rather than private-sector ones). Worth confirming with your plan administrator.

It all started with a question that many of us in uniform eventually face — the need to tap into tomorrow's safety net to cover today's fire. Since you're a private-sector firefighter, let me lay out the tax landscape clearly, because early withdrawals from a retirement plan can bite hard if you're not prepared.

**The two big federal taxes to expect:**

1. **Ordinary income tax.** Any amount you withdraw from a traditional 401(k) or traditional IRA is generally taxed as ordinary income in the year you take it. That stacks on top of your firefighter salary, so it can push you into a higher bracket and raise your overall tax bill.

2. **The 10% early-distribution penalty.** If you're under age 59½, the IRS typically adds a 10% penalty on top of the income tax. So a $20,000 withdrawal could cost you $2,000 in penalties alone, plus whatever income tax applies.

**Important exceptions to the penalty (not the income tax):**
- A **qualified public safety employee** who separates from service in or after the year they turn **age 50** may avoid the 10% penalty on 401(k)/403(b)/governmental 457(b) distributions. Note the fine print: this age-50 rule applies to *qualified public safety employees*, and depending on your plan type, private-sector firefighters may or may not fit the definition the IRS uses — this is worth confirming with your plan administrator and a tax professional.
- Governmental **457(b)** plans are a notable exception — they generally don't impose the 10% early-withdrawal penalty at all, though income tax still applies.
- Other exceptions include certain medical expenses, qualified birth/adoption, total disability, and a few others.

**Things that could soften the blow:**
- **Roth accounts** work differently — you've already paid tax on contributions, so qualified withdrawals of contributions are tax-free, but earnings can still be taxed and penalized if you're under 59½.
- **A 401(k) loan** (if your plan allows it) avoids taxes and penalties entirely if repaid on schedule.
- **Rollovers** to another retirement account aren't taxable events if done correctly.

**A couple of cautions:**
- Your plan may allow withdrawals only for specific hardship reasons, and it may withhold 20% for federal tax upfront on certain distributions.
- Your state may add its own income tax and possibly its own penalty.

Given that you're drawing a salary and juggling shift work and possibly overtime, the bracket jump is a real risk — a withdrawal in a high-earning year can be expensive. Before you move, I'd strongly suggest running the numbers with a CPA or tax pro who knows your state's rules and your plan type, and also checking whether a loan or a different savings source might get you through without the tax hit.

If you tell me the type of plan (401(k), 403(b), 457(b), traditional or Roth IRA) and roughly how much you're considering, I can walk you through a more specific estimate.

question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.

Yes — early withdrawals from retirement plans generally come with significant tax consequences. Here's what you should be aware of:

## 1. Income Tax on the Withdrawal
Any amount you withdraw from a **traditional 401(k) or traditional IRA** is taxed as **ordinary income** in the year you take it. Your plan administrator will typically withhold 20% for federal taxes, but that may not cover your full tax bill depending on your bracket.

*(Note: **Roth** withdrawals of contributions are generally tax-free, but earnings withdrawn before age 59½ may be taxable.)*

## 2. The 10% Early Distribution Penalty
If you're **under age 59½**, you'll generally owe an additional **10% penalty** on the taxable portion of the withdrawal. This is on top of regular income tax.

**Example:** Withdraw $10,000 → you could owe roughly $2,200–$3,700+ in federal income tax (depending on bracket) **plus** a $1,000 penalty.

## 3. Exceptions to the 10% Penalty
The penalty (not the income tax) may be waived in certain cases, including:
- Qualified birth or adoption expenses (up to $5,000)
- Certain medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of AGI
- Permanent disability
- First-time home purchase (IRA only, up to $10,000)
- Qualified higher education expenses (IRA only)
- Unreimbursed medical premiums while unemployed
- Certain federally declared disaster distributions
- Birth/adoption, terminal illness, or domestic abuse exceptions (up to limits)

## 4. State Taxes
Most states also tax the distribution and some impose their **own additional penalty** (often 2.5%–10%). Your state's rules matter.

## 5. Other Things to Watch
- **Withholding may be insufficient** — you may owe more at tax time.
- **It can push you into a higher bracket** or affect other income-tested items (e.g., ACA subsidies, Medicare IRMAA).
- **You lose future tax-deferred growth** on the withdrawn amount.
- **60-day rollover rule:** If you can replace the funds within 60 days (and it's an eligible rollover), you can avoid tax/penalty — but the 20% withheld must be made up out of pocket.

## Before You Withdraw
- Check whether your plan allows **loans** (no tax if repaid) instead of a withdrawal.
- Review **hardship distributions** vs. normal distributions.
- Consider **Roth conversion or 72(t) substantially equal periodic payments** for penalty-free access.

⚠️ **Important:** I'm not a tax professional, and the rules depend heavily on your plan type, age, state, and personal situation. I'd strongly recommend consulting a **CPA or tax advisor** and possibly your plan administrator before withdrawing — a small planning step now can save you a large tax bill later.

If you tell me your **age, plan type (401k/IRA/Roth), and state**, I can give you a more specific idea of what to expect.

**1. Early Withdrawal Penalty**
- If you're under age 59½, most retirement plans (401(k), traditional IRA, etc.) impose a **10% additional tax penalty** on the amount withdrawn, on top of regular income tax.

**2. Ordinary Income Tax**
- The withdrawn amount is generally treated as **ordinary income** in the year you take it, taxed at your marginal rate. This can bump you into a higher bracket and affect other tax items.

**3. Exceptions to the 10% Penalty**
Certain situations may waive the penalty (though income tax still applies):
- Qualified first-time home purchase (up to $10,000 for IRAs)
- Qualified higher education expenses (IRAs)
- Certain medical expenses exceeding a percentage of AGI
- Permanent disability or death

**4. Plan-Specific Rules**
- **401(k)s**: Many employers don't allow in-service withdrawals while you're still employed. Also, 401(k) mandatory 20% withholding may apply to the taxable portion.
- **Roth IRAs**: You can withdraw your *contributions* tax- and penalty-free anytime, but *earnings* are subject to the rules above.
- **Roth 401(k)**: Different rules than Roth IRA—generally follows the 401(k) framework.

**5. State Taxes**
- Some states also impose their own penalty or tax treatment, so check your state's rules.

**6. Impact on Retirement Savings**
- Beyond taxes, you lose the future tax-deferred growth on that money, which can be substantial over time.

content:
Since you're an active duty service member, there are some important protections and considerations specific to you that are worth knowing before you apply for a loan:

**1. The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA)**
This is the big one. The SCRA caps the interest rate on debts you incurred *before* entering active duty (or before you were called to active duty) at **6%** while you're on active duty. If a lender charges more, you can request the excess be forgiven. Note: this applies to pre-service debts, not loans you take out now — but if you have older debts, it's worth checking.

**2. The Military Lending Act (MLA)**
This directly protects you on *new* loans. The MLA caps the **Military Annual Percentage Rate (MAPR) at 36%** on most consumer loans, including payday loans, vehicle title loans, deposit advance loans, and (with some exceptions) credit cards and installment loans. It also prohibits:
- Mandatory arbitration clauses
- Prepayment penalties
- Requiring allotments as a condition of the loan

Because you're active duty, most lenders must give you these protections — but some products (like mortgages, and certain vehicle or personal loans in specific circumstances) fall outside the MLA's coverage, so the 36% cap doesn't apply to everything.

**3. Watch for predatory lending**
Lenders sometimes target service members specifically because of steady military pay and housing/COLA entitlements. Be wary of:
- Loans advertised near base
- "No credit check" offers with sky-high fees
- Pressure to use your military allotment as repayment

**4. Credit and debt-to-income**
A new loan adds to your debt-to-income ratio, which affects both this loan's approval and any future ones. Also, if you're planning a PCS, deployment, or a security clearance review down the line, high debt loads can raise flags — so it's worth keeping your borrowing conservative.

**5. Don't forget your base resources**
Your installation's **Personal Financial Management Program** or Military OneSource offer free financial counseling. They can review a loan offer before you sign — no cost, no pressure.

A couple of questions that would help me tailor this:
- What kind of loan are you considering (auto, personal, VA mortgage, etc.)?
- Is this a loan you'd be taking out while on active duty, or are you comparing to pre-service debt?

If you have any dependents or specific financial obligations you're juggling, that's also worth factoring in. Want me to go deeper on any of these?

Since I don’t have any stored information about your finances, goals, or personal circumstances, I’ll keep this general—but here are the main things to be aware of before applying for a loan:

**1. Check your credit reports and scores first**
- In the U.S., you can get free reports from AnnualCreditReport.com.
- Look for errors, late payments, high balances, or accounts that aren’t yours. Disputing errors before applying can improve your approval odds and terms.
- Know which score the lender likely uses—mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards can weigh things differently.

**2. Understand the full cost, not just the monthly payment**
- Compare the **APR**, not just the interest rate. APR includes fees.
- Ask about origination fees, closing costs, prepayment penalties, late fees, and any insurance requirements.
- Calculate the **total amount you’ll repay** over the life of the loan.

**3. Shop around—but do it strategically**
- Multiple inquiries in a short window for the same type of loan (like mortgages or auto loans) are often treated as one inquiry by scoring models.
- Get quotes from several lenders, including banks, credit unions, and online lenders.
- Credit unions sometimes offer lower rates, especially for members.

**4. Borrow only what you need**
- It’s tempting to take a higher limit “just in case,” but you’ll pay interest on it.
- For secured loans, remember the collateral is at risk if you default.

**5. Watch the debt-to-income ratio**
- Lenders look at how much of your monthly income goes toward debt payments.
- Paying down existing debt or increasing income before applying can help.

**6. Be cautious with these**
- **Payday loans, title loans, and high-cost installment loans** can have APRs of 300%+ and trap borrowers in cycles of debt.
- **“Guaranteed approval”** offers often come with very high costs.
- **Co-signing** means you’re fully responsible if the other person doesn’t pay.

**7. Prepare your documents**
- Proof of income, ID, bank statements, employment info, and sometimes tax returns.
- Self-employed borrowers often need more documentation.

**8. Ask about hardship options before you sign**
- What happens if you lose your job or have a medical emergency?
- Are there deferment, forbearance, or modification options?

**9. Avoid new credit inquiries or big changes right before applying**
- Don’t open new credit cards, finance a car, or change jobs right before a major loan application if you can avoid it.

**10. Read the fine print**
- Especially the sections on variable rates, balloon payments, and what triggers default.

**Before you apply**
- **Check your credit score and report.** In the US you can get free reports from AnnualCreditReport.com; in the UK, check Experian, Equifax, or TransUnion. Errors can drag your score down, so dispute anything incorrect before applying.
- **Know your debt-to-income ratio (DTI).** Most lenders like to see it below 36–43%. It's your total monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income.
- **Shop around, but cluster your applications.** Rate-shopping within a short window (typically 14–45 days depending on the loan type and country) usually counts as one hard inquiry, so you can compare without extra damage.

**Understand the loan itself**
- **APR vs. interest rate.** APR includes fees, so it's the truer cost of borrowing.
- **Fixed vs. variable rates.** Variable rates can rise over time — factor that into what you can realistically afford.
- **Total cost, not just monthly payment.** A longer term lowers the payment but can dramatically increase what you pay overall.
- **Fees.** Look for origination fees, prepayment penalties, late fees, and any admin charges.

- Tools to check: WebAIM Contrast Checker, or browser DevTools (Chrome/Firefox both have built-in checkers).
- Pure black (`#000000`) on pure white (`#FFFFFF`) is technically highest contrast, but can feel harsh. Off-black like `#1A1A1A` on off-white is often gentler.

## 2. Choose a Base Palette
- **Body text:** Dark gray on light background (e.g., `#333333` on `#FFFFFF`) is a safe, readable default.
- **Headings:** Can be slightly darker or use a brand color if contrast allows.
- **Links:** Use a distinct color (often blue) plus underline—don't rely on color alone, since colorblind users may miss the cue.

## 3. Don't Rely on Color Alone
- ~8% of men and 0.5% of women have some form of color vision deficiency. Pair color with other visual cues (underline, weight, icons).

## 4. Keep It Consistent
- Limit yourself to 2–3 text colors: one for body, one for headings/accents, one for links.
- Define them as CSS variables so they're easy to tweak system-wide.

## 5. Consider Dark Mode
- Don't just invert—design a separate palette. Pure white text on pure black causes halation (a glowing/bleeding effect). Try `#E0E0E0` text on `#121212` backgrounds.

## 6. Match Your Brand & Mood
- Warm neutrals (browns, creams) feel cozy; cool grays feel modern/techy.
- Blue conveys trust; green suggests growth/health.

## 7. Test in Context
- Check on the actual backgrounds (images, gradients, cards), not just white.
- Test on different screens—colors look different on OLED vs. LCD.

## 1. Prioritize contrast first
The single most important factor is **contrast between text and background**.

- **WCAG minimums:** at least **4.5:1** contrast ratio for normal body text, and **3:1** for large text (roughly 18pt+ or 14pt+ bold).
- **Aim higher for accessibility:** 7:1 (WCAG AAA) is a good target, especially for body copy. Given your low vision, leaning toward the higher end will make reading far more comfortable.
- Tools: **WebAIM Contrast Checker**, **Contrast Ratio** (by Lea Verou), or the built-in contrast checks in Figma/Chrome DevTools.

## 2. Don't use pure black on pure white
`#000000` on `#FFFFFF` technically has maximum contrast, but it can feel harsh and cause eye strain over long reading sessions.

- A softer option: **near-black like `#1A1A1A` or `#212121`** on a **soft white like `#FAFAFA` or `#F5F5F5`**.
- The contrast is still very high, but gentler on the eyes.

## 3. Build a small, deliberate palette
Rather than picking colors ad hoc, define a system:

| Role | Example |
|------|---------|
| Primary text | Near-black `#1F2933` |
| Secondary text | Medium gray `#52606D` |
| Link / accent | A darker blue like `#1D4ED8` (not a light sky blue) |
| Background | Off-white `#FFFFFF` or `#F8F9FA` |

Keep it to 2–3 text colors max, plus one accent for links/interactive elements.

## 4. Links need to stand out beyond color
Roughly **8% of men have some form of color blindness**, so never rely on color alone.

- Underline links, or give them a distinct weight/style.
- Make sure link color also passes contrast against the background (not just against body text).

## 5. Watch these common mistakes
- **Light gray body text** (e.g., `#999999` on white) — very common, and very hard to read.
- **Colored text on colored backgrounds** without checking contrast (e.g., blue on purple).
- **Red/green pairings** for meaning (status, errors) — use icons or labels too.
- **Thin fonts in light colors** — the thinner the stroke, the more contrast you need.

## 6. Test in context
Check your choices on:
- Different screens (phone in sunlight, desktop, etc.)
- **Dark mode**, if you offer it — invert carefully, don't just flip colors (pure white on pure black is also harsh; try `#E8E8E8` on `#121212`).

content:
# Choosing Colors for Website Text

Great topic! Since you've mentioned **low vision**, accessibility should be a top priority for you—both for reading sites and for any you might build.

## The Core Principle: Contrast

The single most important factor is **contrast between text and background**. This matters far more than the specific hue you choose.

- **WCAG standard:** Text should have a contrast ratio of at least **4.5:1** for normal text, and **3:1** for large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold).
- **Aim higher if you can** — 7:1 ("AAA" level) is much more comfortable, especially with low vision.

## Practical Guidelines

1. **Dark text on light background** (or the reverse) is easiest to read. Avoid mid-tone on mid-tone (e.g., gray text on light gray).
2. **Avoid pure black on pure white** for long reading — it can cause halation/glare. A very dark gray (#1a1a1a) on off-white (#f5f5f5) is often gentler. But if high contrast helps *you* personally, pure black/white is fine.
3. **Don't rely on color alone** to convey meaning (e.g., red = error). Add icons, underlines, or text.
4. **Watch out for these common failures:**
   - Light gray placeholder text
   - Thin, light-weight fonts
   - Colored text on colored backgrounds (blue on red, etc.)
5. **Links:** make them distinguishable from body text — commonly blue, but add underline if the contrast isn't obvious.

## Tools to Check Contrast

These let you paste in two colors and get the ratio instantly:

- **WebAIM Contrast Checker** (webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker)
- **Coolors Contrast Checker**
- **Colour Contrast Analyser** (a downloadable desktop app—useful if screen-based tools are tricky for you)
- Browser DevTools (built into Chrome/Firefox) — inspect any text element and it shows the contrast ratio

## For Picking Palettes

- **Coolors.co** — generates palettes and flags accessibility issues
- **Adobe Color** — has a "Color Blind Safe" check
- **Material Design & Tailwind** color scales — pre-tested, accessible defaults

## A Simple Starting Recipe

- Background: `#FFFFFF` or `#F8F9FA`
- Body text: `#212529` (near-black, ~15:1 contrast)
- Links: `#0D6EFD` (blue, underlined)
- Secondary text: `#495057` (still >7:1)

---

**One tip tailored to you:** since contrast checkers are visual, look for ones that **state the ratio as a number** (WebAIM does this) rather than relying on color swatches you have to judge by eye. And if you use a screen reader or magnification, test your final choices in *your* actual setup—what's technically compliant isn't always what's most comfortable.

Would you like help with a specific color pairing you're considering, or recommendations for text/background combos that are known to be easy on low-vision readers?

Since I don't have any stored details about your past trips or preferences, I'll keep this general—but here are the key things to be aware of for a short trip to Canada:

**Entry requirements**
- Most visitors need a valid passport. Depending on your nationality, you may need a **visitor visa** or an **eTA (Electronic Travel Authorization)**. US citizens generally just need a passport for short visits.
- Check your specific country's requirements on the official IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada) website—rules changed for some nationalities in recent years.

**Weather**
- Canada is huge, so conditions vary wildly. Vancouver is mild and rainy; Toronto/Montreal have real seasons; the Prairies and North can be brutally cold. Pack layers and check the forecast for your specific city.

**Money**
- Currency is the **Canadian dollar (CAD)**. Credit cards are widely accepted, but carrying a little cash helps for small shops and tips.
- **Tipping** is expected: ~15–20% at restaurants, a few dollars for hotel housekeeping, etc.

**Getting around**
- Distances are large—flying between cities is often more practical than driving.
- In cities, public transit is good (Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver). Renting a car is best for rural or scenic areas.

**Other practical notes**
- **Sales tax** is added at checkout (varies by province, plus some cities have extra taxes).
- **Mobile plans**: check your roaming; Canadian data can be pricey.
- **Emergency number is 911.**
- **Language**: English everywhere except Quebec, where French is dominant—a friendly "bonjour" goes a long way.

A couple of questions to tailor this:
1. **Which city/region** are you visiting, and **when** (season matters a lot)?
2. **What's your citizenship/passport country**, so I can flag visa vs. eTA?
3. **What's the purpose**—sightseeing, business, visiting family?

If you share those, I can give you much more specific advice. Also—if you have any dietary restrictions, allergies, or health conditions, let me know and I'll factor those in too.

content:
Yes—there are a couple of things worth being aware of, especially given your pending I-485.

**1. Travel while I-485 is pending**
- If you leave the U.S. without proper authorization while your I-485 is pending, USCIS generally treats it as **abandoning your adjustment of status application**—unless you have a valid **Advance Parole** document (Form I-131 approved) in hand *before* you depart.
- So the key question is: **do you have an approved Advance Parole (or a combo card)?** If not, traveling abroad now could jeopardize your green card application. You'd want to either wait for the Advance Parole or consult your immigration attorney before booking.
- If you *do* have Advance Parole, bring it with you and re-enter using it (not just your visa). Keep your I-485 receipt notice handy too.

**2. Canada-specific entry requirements**
- **U.S. green card holders** can enter Canada without a visa for short visits—but since your green card isn't approved yet, that exemption likely doesn't apply to you.
- As an I-485 applicant, you'd generally need a **Canadian visitor visa (TRV)** unless you're a citizen of a visa-exempt country. Check whether your nationality qualifies for an **eTA** or requires a full visa.
- Also note: Canada may ask about your U.S. immigration status, and a pending adjustment can sometimes raise questions at the border.

**3. Re-entry to the U.S.**
- Even with Advance Parole, re-entry isn't 100% guaranteed—CBP officers make the final call. Carry evidence of your pending case (receipt notices, employment letter, etc.).

**Bottom line:** Before you go, confirm you have **Advance Parole** (if you're relying on it) and the **correct Canadian entry document** for your nationality. This is exactly the kind of trip where a quick check with your immigration attorney is worth it, since abandoning your I-485 would be a costly mistake.

Do you know whether you have Advance Parole, and what passport you'll be traveling on? I can give you more specific guidance.

E-2 CNMI
An E-2 CNMI investor is an alien who seeks to enter or remain in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana
Islands (CNMI) in order to maintain an investment in the CNMI that was approved by the CNMI government
prior to November 28, 2009. An E-2 CNMI investor classification is specifically limited to an alien investor who

allows an eligible alien to be lawfully present in the CNMI in order to maintain the investment during the
transition period from CNMI to Federal immigration law. An investor’s nationality is not a qualifying factor in the
issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification.

CNMI investor classification became available, which was January 18, 2011. Petitions for the initial issuance of the E-2
CNMI filed after January 18, 2013 will be rejected.
Requests for extension of the E-2 CNMI investor classification may be granted, in increments of not more than 2 years,
until December 31, 2029.
Applications for the dependents of E-2 CNMI investors must be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change
Nonimmigrant Status.
Write E-2C in the classification block.
The petition must be filed with documentary evidence of:
1. Continuous maintenance of the terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI investor nonimmigrant status;
2. Physical presence in the CNMI at the time of filing of the extension of stay request; and
3. The fact that the beneficiary will not leave during the pendency of the extension of stay request.
H-1B Nonimmigrants (Three Types)
The H-1B classification is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily to perform services in a specialty
occupation.
Write H-1B in the classification block.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 8 of 30
A specialty occupation is one that requires the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized
knowledge to fully perform the occupation and requires the attainment of a bachelor’s or higher degree in a specific
specialty, or its equivalent, as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or a U.S. agent and must be filed with:
1. Evidence that a labor condition application (LCA) has been certified by the U.S. Department of Labor;
2. Evidence showing that the proposed employment qualifies as a specialty occupation;
3. Evidence showing that the beneficiary has the required degree by submitting either:
A. A copy of the beneficiary’s U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree as required by the specialty occupation;
B. A copy of a foreign degree and evidence that it is equivalent to the U.S. degree; or
C. Evidence of education, specialized training, and/or progressively responsible experience that is equivalent to the
required U.S. degree.
4. A copy of any required license or other official permission to practice the occupation in the state of intended
employment; and
5. A copy of any written contract between the petitioner and the beneficiary or a summary of the terms of the oral
agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
6. If you are filing an H-1B cap petition for a fiscal year that H-1B registration is required, you must provide a valid
Beneficiary Confirmation Number for the beneficiary included in this petition, along with a copy of the H-1B
Registration Selection Notice.
NOTE: This evidence requirement is not applicable to H-1B2 petitions.
7. Off-site Assignment of H-1B Beneficiaries: Petitioners seeking to place the H-1B beneficiary off-site at a location
other than their own location must answer general questions regarding this assignment in Part 5., Basic Information
About the Proposed Employment and Employer. Petitioners should advise the H-1B beneficiary of the off-site
work placement.
An H-1B cap-subject petition (including a petition eligible for the advanced degree exemption) only will be accepted for
filing if the underlying registration (or the petition itself, if the registration requirement is suspended) is selected toward
the annual numerical allocations. When applicable, registrations (or petitions) will be ranked and selected based on
the Occupational Employment Survey (OES) wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the
relevant Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code in their area(s) of intended employment. Therefore, in the
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, Item Number 11., you must specify the
highest OES wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s)
of intended employment. The OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES
wage level as of the date that the registration underlying the petition was submitted. However, if the registration process
is suspended, the OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES wage level
as of the date that the petition is filed.
The proffered wage is the wage that you intend to pay the beneficiary as indicated on the petition. The SOC code and
area(s) of intended employment should be indicated on the LCA filed with the petition.
NOTE: If the beneficiary will work in multiple locations, or in multiple positions if you are filing the petition as an agent,
you must select the lowest corresponding OES wage level that the proffered wage will equal or exceed. If the proffered
wage is expressed as a range, you must select the OES wage level based on the lowest wage in the range. If you are
relying on a prevailing wage that is not based on the OES survey, and the proffered wage is less than the corresponding
level I OES wage, you must select the “Wage Level I and below” box. You may not lower the proffered wage listed on the
petition to an amount that would be equivalent to a lower wage level than the wage level reflected on the selected H-1B
registration. If the relevant SOC code does not have current OES prevailing wage information available, you should
follow U.S. Department of Labor guidance on prevailing wage determinations to determine which OES wage level to
select.
The H-1B classification is also for aliens coming to the United States to perform services of an exceptional nature
relating to a cooperative research and development project administered by the U.S. Department of Defense
(DOD).
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 9 of 30
Write H-1B2 in the classification requested block.
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent may file the petition.
The petition must be filed with:
1. A description of the proposed employment;
2. Evidence that the services and project meet the above conditions;
3. A statement listing the names of aliens who are currently or have been employed on the project within the past year,
along with their dates of employment;
4. Evidence that the beneficiary holds a bachelor’s or higher degree or its equivalent in the field of employment; and
5. A verification letter from the DOD project manager. Details about the specific project are not required.

Write H-1B3 in the classification block.

beneficiary will perform services at events or productions of a distinguished reputation. Such evidence includes:
1. Documentary evidence (such as certifications, affidavits, and reviews) to establish the beneficiary is a fashion model
of distinguished merit and ability. Any affidavits submitted by present or former employers or recognized experts
must set forth their expertise of the affiant and the manner in which the affiant acquired such information; and
2. Copies of any written contracts between the petitioner and the beneficiary or, if there is no written agreement, a
summary of the terms of the oral agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.

Three relevant laws impacting the filing of H-1B and/or L visa petitions; include:
1. The American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA), Public Law 105-277 (signed into
law on October 21, 1998);
2. The H-1B Visa Reform Act of 2004 (signed into law on December 8, 2004); and
3. Public Law 114-113 (signed into law on December 18, 2005).

Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, which is part of this petition. We use this supplement (formerly issued separately as
Form I-129W) to collect additional information about the H-1B nonimmigrant workers and the H-1B petitioners, and to
determine the applicability of fees mandated by ACWIA (INA section 214(c)(9)), the H-1B1 Visa Reform Act of 2004
(INA section 214(c)(12)), and Public Law 114-113.
A petitioner seeking initial approval of H-1B or L nonimmigrant status for a beneficiary, or seeking approval to employ an
H-1B or L nonimmigrant currently working for another employer, must submit an additional $500 Fraud Prevention and
Detection fee. This fee does not apply to H-1B1 petitions. The Form I-129 will serve as the vehicle for collection of the
$500 fee.
Those petitioners required to submit the $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee are also required to submit either an
additional $4,000 (H-1B) or $4,500 (L-1) fee mandated by Public Law 114-113, if:
1. The petitioner employs 50 or more individuals in the United States;
2. More than 50 percent of those employees are in H-1B or L-1A or L-1B nonimmigrant status; and
3. The petition is filed on or after December 18, 2015.
The Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee and Public Law 114-113 Fee, when applicable, may not be waived. Each
fee should be submitted by separate check or money order.
To determine if they are subject to any of these fees, petitioners must complete the H-1B and H1B1 Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement discussed below.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 10 of 30
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent who seek to place a beneficiary in H-1B classification (including H-1B1 classification for
free trade aliens from Chile and Singapore) must file this supplement.
The supplement is used to:
1. Collect additional information about the H-1B employer and beneficiary; and
2. Determine the appropriate American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA) fee. The ACWIA
Fee is a training fee meant to fund the training of U.S. workers. But if the employer has 25 or fewer full-time
employees, they must pay only one-half of the required fee at INA 214(c)(9)(B). This supplement also helps to
determine whether the beneficiary is subject to the H-1B numerical limitation (also known as the H-1B Cap). Please
note that the ACWIA fee may not be assessed to the beneficiary.
Who is required to submit this supplement?
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent seeking to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant worker
must file this supplement with the Form I-129 and the appropriate fee. (See What is the Filing Fee, for more information
about the appropriate fee.)
Completing Section 1. of the H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement Form
All petitioners who seek to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant worker must answer every
question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.

5. A verification letter from the DOD project manager. Details about the specific project are not required.
The H-1B classification is also for aliens of distinguished merit and ability in the field of fashion modeling.
Write H-1B3 in the classification block.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or U.S. agent. The petitioner must submit evidence that establishes the
beneficiary will perform services at events or productions of a distinguished reputation. Such evidence includes:
1. Documentary evidence (such as certifications, affidavits, and reviews) to establish the beneficiary is a fashion model
of distinguished merit and ability. Any affidavits submitted by present or former employers or recognized experts
must set forth their expertise of the affiant and the manner in which the affiant acquired such information; and
2. Copies of any written contracts between the petitioner and the beneficiary or, if there is no written agreement, a
summary of the terms of the oral agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
General H-1B Requirements
Three relevant laws impacting the filing of H-1B and/or L visa petitions; include:
1. The American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA), Public Law 105-277 (signed into
law on October 21, 1998);
2. The H-1B Visa Reform Act of 2004 (signed into law on December 8, 2004); and
3. Public Law 114-113 (signed into law on December 18, 2005).
Because of ACWIA, H-1B and H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant petitioners must complete the H-1B Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, which is part of this petition. We use this supplement (formerly issued separately as
Form I-129W) to collect additional information about the H-1B nonimmigrant workers and the H-1B petitioners, and to
determine the applicability of fees mandated by ACWIA (INA section 214(c)(9)), the H-1B1 Visa Reform Act of 2004
(INA section 214(c)(12)), and Public Law 114-113.
A petitioner seeking initial approval of H-1B or L nonimmigrant status for a beneficiary, or seeking approval to employ an
H-1B or L nonimmigrant currently working for another employer, must submit an additional $500 Fraud Prevention and
Detection fee. This fee does not apply to H-1B1 petitions. The Form I-129 will serve as the vehicle for collection of the
$500 fee.
Those petitioners required to submit the $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee are also required to submit either an
additional $4,000 (H-1B) or $4,500 (L-1) fee mandated by Public Law 114-113, if:
1. The petitioner employs 50 or more individuals in the United States;
2. More than 50 percent of those employees are in H-1B or L-1A or L-1B nonimmigrant status; and
3. The petition is filed on or after December 18, 2015.
The Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee and Public Law 114-113 Fee, when applicable, may not be waived. Each
fee should be submitted by separate check or money order.
To determine if they are subject to any of these fees, petitioners must complete the H-1B and H1B1 Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement discussed below.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 10 of 30
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent who seek to place a beneficiary in H-1B classification (including H-1B1 classification for
free trade aliens from Chile and Singapore) must file this supplement.
The supplement is used to:
1. Collect additional information about the H-1B employer and beneficiary; and
2. Determine the appropriate American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA) fee. The ACWIA
Fee is a training fee meant to fund the training of U.S. workers. But if the employer has 25 or fewer full-time
employees, they must pay only one-half of the required fee at INA 214(c)(9)(B). This supplement also helps to
determine whether the beneficiary is subject to the H-1B numerical limitation (also known as the H-1B Cap). Please
note that the ACWIA fee may not be assessed to the beneficiary.
Who is required to submit this supplement?
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent seeking to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant worker
must file this supplement with the Form I-129 and the appropriate fee. (See What is the Filing Fee, for more information
about the appropriate fee.)
Completing Section 1. of the H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement Form
All petitioners who seek to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant worker must answer every
question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.

content:
Great question — text color is one of the most impactful (and most commonly botched) parts of web design. Here are practical recommendations, from the fundamentals to specific techniques:

## Start with contrast, not color
- **WCAG contrast minimums** are the baseline. For body text, aim for a contrast ratio of at least **4.5:1** against the background; for large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold), **3:1** is acceptable. Ideally aim higher (7:1) for maximum readability.
- Never rely on color alone to convey meaning (e.g., red for errors) — pair it with an icon or label for accessibility.

## Choose a palette structure
- **Pick one base text color, not pure black.** Pure black (#000) on white can feel harsh and causes eye strain. Off-black shades like `#1a1a1a`, `#222`, or a very dark tint of your brand hue read better.
- **Use 2–3 levels of text hierarchy**: a primary color for body, a slightly lighter one for secondary/meta text, and a muted one for disabled states. Keep them all from the same hue family so they feel intentional.
- **Tint, don't gray.** Instead of neutral grays, use dark/light versions of your brand color for a more cohesive look.

## Match text to background properly
- **On light backgrounds**: use dark text; make sure "secondary" grays aren't so light they fail contrast (a common mistake).
- **On dark backgrounds**: avoid pure white (#fff) — it glows. Try `#eee`–`#f5f5f5`, and make sure your text is *lighter* than the background, not just different.
- **Over images or gradients**: add a semi-transparent overlay or text shadow so contrast holds regardless of the photo behind it.

## Practical color choices
- **Links**: make them distinguishable from body text — either a distinct color *or* an underline (best: both). Don't rely on color alone.
- **Avoid saturated colors for long-form text.** Reds, bright blues, and yellows fatigue the eyes. Reserve vivid colors for headings, buttons, and accents.
- **Warm vs. cool**: warm tones (off-white backgrounds, dark browns) feel cozy and editorial; cool tones (slate grays, deep blues) feel clean and techy. Match to your brand's mood.
- **Test in both light and dark mode** if you support it — colors that work on white often fail on dark, and vice versa.

## Tools to help you
- **WebAIM Contrast Checker** and **Coolors Contrast Checker** — instant ratio checks.
- **Coolors.co** or **Adobe Color** — generate harmonious palettes.
- **Stark** (Figma/Sketch plugin) or browser DevTools' built-in contrast auditing.
- Google's **Material Design** and **Tailwind CSS** color scales give you ready-made, tested text hierarchies.

## A quick starting formula
1. Pick your background (e.g., `#ffffff` or `#111827`).
2. Choose a body text color with 7:1+ contrast.
3. Create 1–2 lighter/darker variants for secondary text.
4. Pick one accent color for links/buttons — and underline your links.
5. Run everything through a contrast checker before shipping.

Since you have a pending I-485 green card application, the most important thing to flag is **re-entry risk**: traveling outside the U.S. while an adjustment of status application is pending can be complicated, and in some cases can be treated as abandoning your application if you don't have the right travel document. Here's what you should be aware of:

## 1. Advance Parole (Travel Document)
- If your I-485 is pending, you generally need **Advance Parole (Form I-131)** approved *before* you leave the U.S., unless you're traveling on a valid H-1B, H-4, L-1, or L-2 visa (those are exceptions under USCIS policy).
- Leaving without Advance Parole (and without qualifying for an exception) can cause USCIS to consider your I-485 **abandoned**.
- Even with Advance Parole, re-entry isn't guaranteed — you'll still be inspected by CBP at the border.

## 2. Canada-Specific Entry Requirements
- **U.S. green card holders** can enter Canada without a visa for short visits (usually up to 6 months). But if you're not yet a green card holder and only have a pending application, you'll need to check requirements based on your **current nationality/passport** — many nationalities need a Canadian visa or eTA.
- U.S. lawful permanent residents generally need to carry their **green card (Form I-551)** and passport to re-enter the U.S.

## 3. Documents to Carry
- Passport
- Advance Parole document (if applicable) or valid visa
- Your I-485 receipt notice (useful as backup)
- Any other immigration documents

## 4. Other General Notes
- **Health/medications**: If you take prescription medication, bring it in original labeled containers.
- **Your foot pain / digestive issues**: If you're dealing with ongoing symptoms, consider whether travel (long sitting, different food, etc.) might aggravate them, and pack accordingly.
- **Weather/season**: Canada varies hugely by region — pack for the specific area and season.

## Bottom Line
Before booking anything, **confirm with your immigration attorney** whether you can travel and what document you need. This is a case where getting it wrong can seriously affect your green card case. If you don't have an attorney, consider a quick consultation — it's worth it given your pending I-485.

Want me to go deeper on any part — like Advance Parole timing, or Canada's entry rules for your specific situation?

Choosing text colors for a website is really about two things: **readability** (can people comfortably read it?) and **mood/brand** (does it feel right for your site?). Here's a practical framework you can apply, and I'll tie it to your Wild Mushroom Lights store since you already have a shop to work with.

## 1. Start with contrast, not color
The single most important rule is **contrast ratio**. WCAG (the web accessibility standard) sets the bar:
- **4.5:1 minimum** for normal body text
- **3:1 minimum** for large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold)

Free tools to check:
- **WebAIM Contrast Checker** (webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker)
- **Coolors Contrast Checker**
- The built-in contrast checker in Chrome/Firefox DevTools

Never rely on your eyes alone — dark gray on light gray *looks* fine until someone with low vision tries to read it.

## 2. Build a small, disciplined palette
You don't need many colors. A typical scheme:

| Role | Suggested approach |
|------|-------------------|
| **Body text** | Near-black, not pure black (e.g., `#1a1a1a` or `#222`) — softer, less harsh on screens |
| **Secondary text** | Muted gray (e.g., `#666` / `#767676` minimum for accessibility) |
| **Headings** | Often same as body, or your brand accent |
| **Links** | One distinct accent color, consistent everywhere |
| **Background** | Usually off-white (`#fafafa`, `#f5f5f5`) rather than pure white |

**Key insight:** use *shades of the same hue* for neutrals (greys with a slight warm or cool tint) so the page feels cohesive rather than flat.

## 3. Think in hue relationships
Basic color-harmony strategies:
- **Monochromatic** — one hue, varied lightness. Clean, safe, elegant.
- **Analogous** — neighboring hues on the color wheel. Calm, harmonious.
- **Complementary** — opposite hues. High energy, great for accent/CTA buttons.
- **Triadic** — three evenly spaced hues. Playful, harder to balance.

**60-30-10 rule:** 60% dominant (background), 30% secondary (text/structure), 10% accent (buttons, links). It keeps things from feeling busy.

## 4. Test across modes and backgrounds
Text that works on white may fail on an image or dark section. Define separate text colors for:
- Light backgrounds
- Dark backgrounds
- Colored overlays (e.g., text over a photo — often needs a scrim/shadow)

## Suggested palette for your mushroom light store
Since your product is *night lights* — glowing, warm, organic — a palette evoking forest + ambient glow tends to work well:

- **Background:** soft warm off-white `#FAF7F2` or deep charcoal `#1C1B18` for dark mode
- **Body text:** `#2B2724` (warm near-black) on light / `#EDE7DD` on dark
- **Accent (links, buttons):** warm amber `#D98A2B` or mossy green `#5A6B44`
- **Secondary text:** `#6E6559`

Test amber `#D98A2B` on your off-white — it may need darkening for body-size text to hit 4.5:1, so reserve bright amber for large headings and use a deeper tone for links.

## 5. Small habits that make a big difference
- **Limit link color** to one accent used consistently.
- **Don't use color alone** to convey meaning (add underline to links).
- **Avoid pure red/green combinations** for text — colorblind users struggle.
- **Reuse tokens**: define your palette once (CSS variables) so text colors stay consistent across pages.

---

Since you're already building out your website and want a community page, this ties in nicely: a tight, accessible palette will make both the store and the community section feel like one coherent brand.

Want me to help you build an actual CSS variable palette (with hex codes verified for contrast) for the store — or a dark-mode version? I can also suggest a couple of free color palette tools (Coolors, Adobe Color, Realtime Colors) if you'd like to experiment visually.

An E-2 CNMI investor is an alien who seeks to enter or remain in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana
Islands (CNMI) in order to maintain an investment in the CNMI that was approved by the CNMI government
prior to November 28, 2009. An E-2 CNMI investor classification is specifically limited to an alien investor who

CNMI investor classification became available, which was January 18, 2011. Petitions for the initial issuance of the E-2
CNMI filed after January 18, 2013 will be rejected.
Requests for extension of the E-2 CNMI investor classification may be granted, in increments of not more than 2 years,
until December 31, 2029.
Applications for the dependents of E-2 CNMI investors must be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change
Nonimmigrant Status.
Write E-2C in the classification block.
The petition must be filed with documentary evidence of:
1. Continuous maintenance of the terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI investor nonimmigrant status;
2. Physical presence in the CNMI at the time of filing of the extension of stay request; and
3. The fact that the beneficiary will not leave during the pendency of the extension of stay request.
H-1B Nonimmigrants (Three Types)
The H-1B classification is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily to perform services in a specialty
occupation.
Write H-1B in the classification block.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 8 of 30
A specialty occupation is one that requires the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized
knowledge to fully perform the occupation and requires the attainment of a bachelor’s or higher degree in a specific
specialty, or its equivalent, as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or a U.S. agent and must be filed with:
1. Evidence that a labor condition application (LCA) has been certified by the U.S. Department of Labor;
2. Evidence showing that the proposed employment qualifies as a specialty occupation;
3. Evidence showing that the beneficiary has the required degree by submitting either:
A. A copy of the beneficiary’s U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree as required by the specialty occupation;
B. A copy of a foreign degree and evidence that it is equivalent to the U.S. degree; or
C. Evidence of education, specialized training, and/or progressively responsible experience that is equivalent to the
required U.S. degree.
4. A copy of any required license or other official permission to practice the occupation in the state of intended
employment; and
5. A copy of any written contract between the petitioner and the beneficiary or a summary of the terms of the oral
agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
6. If you are filing an H-1B cap petition for a fiscal year that H-1B registration is required, you must provide a valid
Beneficiary Confirmation Number for the beneficiary included in this petition, along with a copy of the H-1B

NOTE: This evidence requirement is not applicable to H-1B2 petitions.
7. Off-site Assignment of H-1B Beneficiaries: Petitioners seeking to place the H-1B beneficiary off-site at a location
other than their own location must answer general questions regarding this assignment in Part 5., Basic Information
About the Proposed Employment and Employer. Petitioners should advise the H-1B beneficiary of the off-site
work placement.
An H-1B cap-subject petition (including a petition eligible for the advanced degree exemption) only will be accepted for
filing if the underlying registration (or the petition itself, if the registration requirement is suspended) is selected toward
the annual numerical allocations. When applicable, registrations (or petitions) will be ranked and selected based on
the Occupational Employment Survey (OES) wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the
relevant Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code in their area(s) of intended employment. Therefore, in the
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, Item Number 11., you must specify the
highest OES wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s)

wage level as of the date that the registration underlying the petition was submitted. However, if the registration process
is suspended, the OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES wage level
as of the date that the petition is filed.
The proffered wage is the wage that you intend to pay the beneficiary as indicated on the petition. The SOC code and
area(s) of intended employment should be indicated on the LCA filed with the petition.
NOTE: If the beneficiary will work in multiple locations, or in multiple positions if you are filing the petition as an agent,
you must select the lowest corresponding OES wage level that the proffered wage will equal or exceed. If the proffered
wage is expressed as a range, you must select the OES wage level based on the lowest wage in the range. If you are
relying on a prevailing wage that is not based on the OES survey, and the proffered wage is less than the corresponding
level I OES wage, you must select the “Wage Level I and below” box. You may not lower the proffered wage listed on the
petition to an amount that would be equivalent to a lower wage level than the wage level reflected on the selected H-1B
registration. If the relevant SOC code does not have current OES prevailing wage information available, you should
follow U.S. Department of Labor guidance on prevailing wage determinations to determine which OES wage level to

General H-1B Requirements
Three relevant laws impacting the filing of H-1B and/or L visa petitions; include:
1. The American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA), Public Law 105-277 (signed into
law on October 21, 1998);
2. The H-1B Visa Reform Act of 2004 (signed into law on December 8, 2004); and
3. Public Law 114-113 (signed into law on December 18, 2005).
Because of ACWIA, H-1B and H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant petitioners must complete the H-1B Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, which is part of this petition. We use this supplement (formerly issued separately as
Form I-129W) to collect additional information about the H-1B nonimmigrant workers and the H-1B petitioners, and to
determine the applicability of fees mandated by ACWIA (INA section 214(c)(9)), the H-1B1 Visa Reform Act of 2004
(INA section 214(c)(12)), and Public Law 114-113.
A petitioner seeking initial approval of H-1B or L nonimmigrant status for a beneficiary, or seeking approval to employ an
H-1B or L nonimmigrant currently working for another employer, must submit an additional $500 Fraud Prevention and
Detection fee. This fee does not apply to H-1B1 petitions. The Form I-129 will serve as the vehicle for collection of the
$500 fee.

additional $4,000 (H-1B) or $4,500 (L-1) fee mandated by Public Law 114-113, if:
1. The petitioner employs 50 or more individuals in the United States;
2. More than 50 percent of those employees are in H-1B or L-1A or L-1B nonimmigrant status; and
3. The petition is filed on or after December 18, 2015.
The Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee and Public Law 114-113 Fee, when applicable, may not be waived. Each
fee should be submitted by separate check or money order.
To determine if they are subject to any of these fees, petitioners must complete the H-1B and H1B1 Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement discussed below.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 10 of 30
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent who seek to place a beneficiary in H-1B classification (including H-1B1 classification for
free trade aliens from Chile and Singapore) must file this supplement.
The supplement is used to:
1. Collect additional information about the H-1B employer and beneficiary; and
2. Determine the appropriate American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA) fee. The ACWIA
Fee is a training fee meant to fund the training of U.S. workers. But if the employer has 25 or fewer full-time
employees, they must pay only one-half of the required fee at INA 214(c)(9)(B). This supplement also helps to
determine whether the beneficiary is subject to the H-1B numerical limitation (also known as the H-1B Cap). Please
note that the ACWIA fee may not be assessed to the beneficiary.
Who is required to submit this supplement?
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent seeking to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant worker
must file this supplement with the Form I-129 and the appropriate fee. (See What is the Filing Fee, for more information
about the appropriate fee.)
Completing Section 1. of the H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement Form
All petitioners who seek to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant worker must answer every
question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.
