Part 1. Petition Always Required
The following classifications always require a petition.
The initial evidence listed below and the initial evidence listed under the instructions for a change of status or extension of
stay must be included with a petition for a new or concurrent employment or for an extension where there is a change in
previously approved employment.
However, a petition for extension based on unchanged, previously approved employment should only be filed with the
initial evidence required in the extension of stay instructions.
E-2 CNMI
An E-2 CNMI investor is an alien who seeks to enter or remain in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana
Islands (CNMI) in order to maintain an investment in the CNMI that was approved by the CNMI government
prior to November 28, 2009. An E-2 CNMI investor classification is specifically limited to an alien investor who
has previously been granted a qualifying long term investor status under the laws of the CNMI. This classification
allows an eligible alien to be lawfully present in the CNMI in order to maintain the investment during the
transition period from CNMI to Federal immigration law. An investor’s nationality is not a qualifying factor in the
issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification.
This classification expires on December 31, 2029
A petition for the initial issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification must be filed within 2 years of the date the E-2
CNMI investor classification became available, which was January 18, 2011. Petitions for the initial issuance of the E-2
CNMI filed after January 18, 2013 will be rejected.
Requests for extension of the E-2 CNMI investor classification may be granted, in increments of not more than 2 years,
until December 31, 2029.
Applications for the dependents of E-2 CNMI investors must be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change
Nonimmigrant Status.
Write E-2C in the classification block.
The petition must be filed with documentary evidence of:
1. Continuous maintenance of the terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI investor nonimmigrant status;
2. Physical presence in the CNMI at the time of filing of the extension of stay request; and
3. The fact that the beneficiary will not leave during the pendency of the extension of stay request.
H-1B Nonimmigrants (Three Types)
The H-1B classification is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily to perform services in a specialty
occupation.
Write H-1B in the classification block.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 8 of 30
A specialty occupation is one that requires the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized
knowledge to fully perform the occupation and requires the attainment of a bachelor’s or higher degree in a specific
specialty, or its equivalent, as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or a U.S. agent and must be filed with:
1. Evidence that a labor condition application (LCA) has been certified by the U.S. Department of Labor;
2. Evidence showing that the proposed employment qualifies as a specialty occupation;
3. Evidence showing that the beneficiary has the required degree by submitting either:
A. A copy of the beneficiary’s U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree as required by the specialty occupation;
B. A copy of a foreign degree and evidence that it is equivalent to the U.S. degree; or
C. Evidence of education, specialized training, and/or progressively responsible experience that is equivalent to the
required U.S. degree.
4. A copy of any required license or other official permission to practice the occupation in the state of intended
employment; and
5. A copy of any written contract between the petitioner and the beneficiary or a summary of the terms of the oral
agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
6. If you are filing an H-1B cap petition for a fiscal year that H-1B registration is required, you must provide a valid
Beneficiary Confirmation Number for the beneficiary included in this petition, along with a copy of the H-1B
Registration Selection Notice.
NOTE: This evidence requirement is not applicable to H-1B2 petitions.
7. Off-site Assignment of H-1B Beneficiaries: Petitioners seeking to place the H-1B beneficiary off-site at a location
other than their own location must answer general questions regarding this assignment in Part 5., Basic Information
About the Proposed Employment and Employer. Petitioners should advise the H-1B beneficiary of the off-site
work placement.
An H-1B cap-subject petition (including a petition eligible for the advanced degree exemption) only will be accepted for
filing if the underlying registration (or the petition itself, if the registration requirement is suspended) is selected toward
the annual numerical allocations. When applicable, registrations (or petitions) will be ranked and selected based on
the Occupational Employment Survey (OES) wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the
relevant Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code in their area(s) of intended employment. Therefore, in the
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, Item Number 11., you must specify the
highest OES wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s)
of intended employment. The OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES
wage level as of the date that the registration underlying the petition was submitted. However, if the registration process
is suspended, the OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES wage level
as of the date that the petition is filed.
The proffered wage is the wage that you intend to pay the beneficiary as indicated on the petition. The SOC code and
area(s) of intended employment should be indicated on the LCA filed with the petition.
NOTE: If the beneficiary will work in multiple locations, or in multiple positions if you are filing the petition as an agent,
you must select the lowest corresponding OES wage level that the proffered wage will equal or exceed. If the proffered
wage is expressed as a range, you must select the OES wage level based on the lowest wage in the range. If you are
relying on a prevailing wage that is not based on the OES survey, and the proffered wage is less than the corresponding
level I OES wage, you must select the “Wage Level I and below” box. You may not lower the proffered wage listed on the
petition to an amount that would be equivalent to a lower wage level than the wage level reflected on the selected H-1B
registration. If the relevant SOC code does not have current OES prevailing wage information available, you should
follow U.S. Department of Labor guidance on prevailing wage determinations to determine which OES wage level to
select.
The H-1B classification is also for aliens coming to the United States to perform services of an exceptional nature
relating to a cooperative research and development project administered by the U.S. Department of Defense
(DOD).
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 9 of 30
Write H-1B2 in the classification requested block.
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent may file the petition.
The petition must be filed with:
1. A description of the proposed employment;
2. Evidence that the services and project meet the above conditions;
3. A statement listing the names of aliens who are currently or have been employed on the project within the past year,

4. Evidence that the beneficiary holds a bachelor’s or higher degree or its equivalent in the field of employment; and
5. A verification letter from the DOD project manager. Details about the specific project are not required.
The H-1B classification is also for aliens of distinguished merit and ability in the field of fashion modeling.
Write H-1B3 in the classification block.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or U.S. agent. The petitioner must submit evidence that establishes the
beneficiary will perform services at events or productions of a distinguished reputation. Such evidence includes:
1. Documentary evidence (such as certifications, affidavits, and reviews) to establish the beneficiary is a fashion model

2. Copies of any written contracts between the petitioner and the beneficiary or, if there is no written agreement, a
summary of the terms of the oral agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
General H-1B Requirements
Three relevant laws impacting the filing of H-1B and/or L visa petitions; include:
1. The American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA), Public Law 105-277 (signed into
law on October 21, 1998);
2. The H-1B Visa Reform Act of 2004 (signed into law on December 8, 2004); and
3. Public Law 114-113 (signed into law on December 18, 2005).
Because of ACWIA, H-1B and H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant petitioners must complete the H-1B Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, which is part of this petition. We use this supplement (formerly issued separately as
Form I-129W) to collect additional information about the H-1B nonimmigrant workers and the H-1B petitioners, and to
determine the applicability of fees mandated by ACWIA (INA section 214(c)(9)), the H-1B1 Visa Reform Act of 2004
(INA section 214(c)(12)), and Public Law 114-113.
A petitioner seeking initial approval of H-1B or L nonimmigrant status for a beneficiary, or seeking approval to employ an
H-1B or L nonimmigrant currently working for another employer, must submit an additional $500 Fraud Prevention and
Detection fee. This fee does not apply to H-1B1 petitions. The Form I-129 will serve as the vehicle for collection of the
$500 fee.
Those petitioners required to submit the $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee are also required to submit either an
additional $4,000 (H-1B) or $4,500 (L-1) fee mandated by Public Law 114-113, if:
1. The petitioner employs 50 or more individuals in the United States;
2. More than 50 percent of those employees are in H-1B or L-1A or L-1B nonimmigrant status; and
3. The petition is filed on or after December 18, 2015.
The Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee and Public Law 114-113 Fee, when applicable, may not be waived. Each
fee should be submitted by separate check or money order.
To determine if they are subject to any of these fees, petitioners must complete the H-1B and H1B1 Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement discussed below.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 10 of 30
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent who seek to place a beneficiary in H-1B classification (including H-1B1 classification for
free trade aliens from Chile and Singapore) must file this supplement.
The supplement is used to:
1. Collect additional information about the H-1B employer and beneficiary; and
2. Determine the appropriate American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA) fee. The ACWIA
Fee is a training fee meant to fund the training of U.S. workers. But if the employer has 25 or fewer full-time
employees, they must pay only one-half of the required fee at INA 214(c)(9)(B). This supplement also helps to
determine whether the beneficiary is subject to the H-1B numerical limitation (also known as the H-1B Cap). Please
note that the ACWIA fee may not be assessed to the beneficiary.
Who is required to submit this supplement?
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent seeking to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant worker
must file this supplement with the Form I-129 and the appropriate fee. (See What is the Filing Fee, for more information
about the appropriate fee.)
Completing Section 1. of the H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement Form
All petitioners who seek to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant worker must answer every
question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.

Sure! Wine tastings can feel intimidating at first, but a few simple habits will make it much more enjoyable. Here are some beginner tips:

**Before you go**
- **Eat something first.** Don't arrive hungry — food helps you pace yourself and keeps your palate steady.
- **Skip strong smells.** Avoid perfume, cologne, or heavily scented lotion; they interfere with both your own and others' ability to smell the wine.
- **Plan for a safe ride.** Spit buckets exist for a reason, and even small pours add up over a flight. Have a designated driver or rideshare.

**At the tasting**
- **Look, swirl, smell, sip.** Tilt the glass against a white background to check the color, swirl to release aromas, take a good sniff, then sip slowly.
- **Actually use the spit bucket.** It's completely normal and expected — it's not rude, and it lets you taste more without getting tipsy.
- **Trust your own palate.** There are no wrong answers. If you taste "green apple" and the person next to you says "pear," you're both right. Describing what *you* notice is the whole point.
- **Take notes.** Jot down what you liked (or didn't). It's the fastest way to learn your preferences.
- **Ask questions.** Pourers and hosts love curious beginners. Ask about the grape, the region, or why a wine tastes the way it does.
- **Start light, move to bold.** If you're tasting several, begin with whites and lighter reds before heavier, tannic ones — big wines can overwhelm your palate.

**A couple of practical notes**
- **Water and bread/crackers** between pours reset your palate.
- **Tannins** (that drying, grippy feeling) are common in reds — not a flaw, just a style. If they bother you, look for lighter reds like Pinot Noir or Gamay.
- **Don't feel pressured to finish anything.** Pouring out a wine you don't like is perfectly fine.

One thing worth flagging: since you've mentioned experimenting with peppers and hot sauce, just be aware that **very spicy or strongly flavored food shortly before a tasting can dull your palate** — so maybe save the habanero-level stuff for after the event.

Mothballs aren't the best fix here, and I'd actually caution against them for a couple of reasons:

**Why to be cautious with mothballs:**
- They're a pesticide (usually containing naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene), and the fumes are a health concern—especially with prolonged inhalation in a small, enclosed space like a closet. They can irritate eyes, nose, and throat and aren't great for anyone with asthma or other respiratory issues.
- The smell is strong and lingers on clothing, which is the opposite of what you want.
- If you have pets or small children, mothballs are especially risky—ingestion is toxic.

**Better approach for a musty closet:**

1. **Find the source of the moisture.** Mustiness = dampness. Check for leaks, poor ventilation, or a humid area behind/beneath the closet. Fixing this solves the root problem.

2. **Air it out.** Empty the closet as much as possible and leave the doors open with a fan running for a day or two.

3. **Clean the surfaces.** Wipe down walls, shelves, and the floor with a diluted white vinegar solution (vinegar is great at killing mold and mildew).

4. **Dry it thoroughly.** A dehumidifier or moisture absorber (like silica gel packs or a DampRid container) works well in closets.

5. **Use a safer freshener.** Cedar blocks or chips, activated charcoal bags, or baking soda boxes absorb odor without harsh chemicals. Cedar also naturally deters moths, if that's part of your concern.

6. **Wash stored clothing.** Anything that already smells musty should be laundered or dry-cleaned, and make sure it's fully dry before hanging back up.

If dampness keeps returning no matter what, it's worth checking for a hidden leak or ventilation issue—that's the real culprit. Want me to go into more detail on any of these steps?

content:
I'd hold off on the mothballs. They contain naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene, which are pretty harsh—they off-gas fumes that can cause headaches, dizziness, and respiratory irritation, and the smell lingers on clothes. For a musty closet, you're better off addressing the root cause (likely moisture) than masking it.

A few things that actually work:

**Fix the moisture**
- Musty smell is usually a sign of dampness. Check for leaks, condensation on walls, or poor airflow.
- Use a **dehumidifier** or **DampRid/moisture absorber** in the closet.
- Keep the closet door open periodically and don't pack clothes so tightly that air can't circulate.

**Clean the source**
- Wash or dry-clean the clothes that smell musty (vapor from cleaning can help reset them).
- Wipe down shelves and walls with a diluted white vinegar solution, then let them dry fully.

**Better odor control than mothballs**
- **Cedar blocks or sachets** — repel insects naturally and smell pleasant.
- **Activated charcoal bags** or **baking soda boxes** — absorb odors without fumes.
- **Lavender or cedar sachets** — gentle and safe.
- If you're dealing with actual moths (holes in clothes), **pheromone traps** and airtight storage bags are far safer than mothballs.

Two safety notes relevant to you specifically:

1. **Mothball fumes aren't great with your G6PD deficiency context either** — while the main G6PD concern is with certain drugs and foods (like fava beans), avoiding unnecessary chemical exposures is a reasonable general precaution, and naphthalene is a known toxin regardless.
2. Since you've mentioned **digestive issues and generally being mindful of what you're exposed to**, keeping harsh volatile chemicals out of your bedroom/closet air is a sensible default.

If the mustiness persists after drying things out, that's worth investigating for hidden mold—especially since you spend time in that space. Want help troubleshooting where the moisture's coming from?

content:
Mothballs would cover up the smell, but I'd gently steer you away from them for a couple of reasons:

**Why to avoid mothballs:**
- They're made of pesticides (naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene) that can be harmful to breathe, especially in an enclosed space like a closet. They can also be a health risk if you have pets or small children who might ingest them.
- They only mask the musty smell rather than fixing the cause.

**Better approach — tackle the root cause:**

1. **Air it out.** Open the closet doors and windows (if possible) and let it breathe for several hours. A fan helps move air through.

2. **Find the moisture source.** Musty = damp. Check for:
   - A leak or condensation on walls/ceiling
   - Damp clothes put away before fully dry
   - Poor ventilation (especially if the closet is on an exterior wall or in a bathroom/humid area)

3. **Dehumidify.** A small dehumidifier or moisture absorber (like DampRid or silica gel packs) works well in closets.

4. **Clean surfaces.** Wipe down shelves, rods, and walls with a mild vinegar-and-water solution, then let dry completely.

5. **Refresh fabrics.** Wash or air out stored clothes, and consider a closet-safe odor absorber like activated charcoal, baking soda, or cedar blocks (cedar also deters moths naturally — a good mothball alternative).

6. **Keep it dry going forward.** Leave a little space between hanging items for airflow, and avoid storing clothes in plastic that traps moisture.

Since you've got that new organic garden going, cedar blocks or lavender sachets would be a nice natural fit for your closet too — and they smell a lot better than mothballs.

opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.

Before you reach for mothballs, I'd actually suggest holding off — and I'll explain why, since it connects to some things you've mentioned before.

**Why to avoid mothballs**
- Mothballs contain **naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene**, which are pesticides. They're a legitimate health concern, especially in enclosed spaces like a closet, and the fumes can irritate your eyes, nose, throat, and lungs.
- They're particularly risky if you have **pets or children** in the home, since the pellets look like candy or treats and are toxic if ingested. (I don't have a note that you have pets, but wanted to flag it in case.)
- They mainly target clothes moths — but musty smell is usually a **moisture/mildew** problem, not a moth problem, so they wouldn't fix the real issue anyway.

**What's actually causing the musty smell (and how to fix it)**
Musty odor almost always means **dampness, poor airflow, or mildew**. So the fix is to address moisture:

1. **Empty the closet and air it out** — leave doors open, ideally with a fan, for a day or two.
2. **Find the moisture source** — check for a leak, a nearby damp wall, or a bathroom on the other side of a wall.
3. **Clean surfaces** — wipe down shelves/walls with a diluted white vinegar solution (or a mild bleach solution if there's visible mildew), then let fully dry.
4. **Wash or air out the clothes** — musty fabric holds the smell; launder washables and air out the rest.
5. **Control humidity** — use a **rechargeable dehumidifier, silica gel packs, or a small damp-rid container**, and keep a gap between clothes and the wall for airflow.
6. **Cedar blocks or lavender sachets** are safe, pleasant-smelling alternatives if you just want the closet to smell nicer.

**Two quick tie-ins to your other projects:**
- Since you've been **decluttering your yarn stash and selling rare yarns online**, this is a great moment to pull anything stored in that closet that's gotten musty — wool and natural fibers are especially prone to mildew, and a musty smell can hurt a sale. Worth sorting before you list.
- If you're **donating old clothes**, give the musty-but-fixable items a wash first; most charities can't accept items with mildew or odor.

Great hobby to get into! Since you're just starting out, I'd recommend easing in with styles that are approachable and help you figure out what you like. Here's a rough path:

**Start here (beginner-friendly):**
- **Blonde Ale / Golden Ale** – Light, crisp, mildly malty. Very easy drinking.
- **Wheat beers (Hefeweizen, Witbier, American Wheat)** – Soft, slightly fruity or spicy, low bitterness. Great gateway beers.
- **Pale Ale** – A step up in hop presence but still balanced and refreshing.
- **Amber / Red Ale** – Toasty malt sweetness with a bit of hop balance. Good for discovering malt flavors.
- **Lager / Pilsner** – Clean and crisp; craft versions often have more flavor than mass-market lagers.

**Then explore (once you know your preferences):**
- **IPA** – The hop-forward flagship of craft beer. Try a hazy/New England IPA if you want juicy and less bitter, or a West Coast IPA if you want piney and bitter.
- **Stout / Porter** – Roasty, chocolatey, coffee notes. Try a milk stout or oatmeal stout for something smoother.
- **Saison / Belgian styles** – Yeasty, spicy, complex. Fun once you want to branch out.
- **Sour / Gose / Berliner Weisse** – Tart and refreshing. An acquired taste for some.

**Practical tips:**
- **Buy single bottles or build-your-own six-packs** so you can sample without committing to a full case.
- **Try flights at breweries or taprooms** — best way to compare styles side by side.
- **Keep notes** (even just in your phone) on what you liked and why. It speeds up finding your palate.
- **Don't chase hype at first.** Start local and fresh; beer is perishable and fresh is usually better.
- **Serve at the right temperature** — too cold mutes flavor, especially for stouts and Belgian styles.

A good first move: grab a mixed six-pack with a blonde, a wheat, a pale ale, an amber, an IPA, and a stout. Taste them over a week and you'll quickly learn whether you lean hoppy, malty, or somewhere in between.

content:
Great question! Craft beer is a fun world to explore.

One important heads-up first: since you've been managing gout for a couple of years, it's worth knowing that **beer — especially beer with high purine content — is one of the more common gout triggers**. Beer yeast is high in purines, and alcohol also reduces your body's ability to excrete uric acid. So if you're going to explore craft beer, it may be worth talking with your doctor about how it fits (or doesn't) into your management plan, and keeping portions small and staying well hydrated when you do indulge. I'd hate for a flare-up to be part of your beer discovery journey.

With that said, here are some styles that are generally friendlier for newcomers to develop your palate:

**Approachable starting points:**
- **Wheat beers (Hefeweizen, Witbier)** — light, cloudy, often with citrus or spice notes. Very easy drinking.
- **Blonde ales & cream ales** — mild, slightly sweet, low bitterness. Good "training wheels."
- **Pilsners & lagers** — crisp and clean. Craft versions are a step up from macro beers without being intimidating.
- **Amber/red ales** — a bit of malt sweetness and toastiness, moderate hops.
- **Pale ales** — more hop character than the above but still balanced. A nice bridge to IPAs.

**Once your palate develops:**
- **IPAs** — the craft staple, but bitter and hop-forward. Try a "hazy" or "New England" IPA first, as they're less bitter and more juicy/fruity.
- **Stouts & porters** — roasty, chocolatey, coffee notes. Avoid the high-ABV imperial versions at first.
- **Saisons & Belgian ales** — fruity, spicy, complex.

**Tips for starting out:**
- Buy single bottles or build-your-own six-packs so you can sample without committing to a full pack.
- Many breweries offer flights — perfect for tasting several styles in small pours (which also keeps your overall intake modest).
- Take notes on what you like; it speeds up finding your lane.

One note on style choice and gout: **avoid or be extra cautious with high-ABV beers and anything particularly yeast-heavy**, and pay attention to how your body responds after you drink. What's a trigger for one person isn't necessarily for another.

- **Serve at the right temp** and use the right glassware if you can; it genuinely changes the experience.
- Don't rush to the extremes (double IPAs, barrel-aged imperial stouts) until your palate adjusts.

content:
Great that you're getting into craft beer! Given your cooking instincts (you're already perfecting a hot sauce, experimenting with peppers, and serving things like mango habanero spritz and spicy mango salsa), you'll probably enjoy exploring beer the same way — by flavor profile rather than by brand.

**Good starter styles, roughly in order of approachability:**

1. **Blonde Ale or Cream Ale** — Light, crisp, mildly malty, very low bitterness. An easy "gateway" beer.
2. **Pale Ale** — A step up in hop presence, but still balanced. American pale ales are citrusy and floral; English ones are earthier and maltier.
3. **Wheat Beer** (Hefeweizen, Witbier, American Wheat) — Cloudy, refreshing, often with banana/clove notes (German) or orange and coriander (Belgian witbier). Very food-friendly; witbier would pair beautifully with your mango salsa.
4. **Amber / Red Ale** — Toasty, caramelly malt with moderate hops. A nice middle ground if pale ales feel too bitter.
5. **Pilsner / Lager** — Clean, crisp, and a good benchmark for what "well-made" tastes like. Czech and German examples are worth seeking out.
6. **Brown Ale** — Nutty and chocolatey without being heavy. Bridges nicely toward darker beers.
7. **Porter** — Roasty and medium-bodied; a gentle introduction to dark beer.
8. **Stout** — Richer and more intense. **Dry Irish stout** (think Guinness) is actually low in alcohol and surprisingly light-bodied — relevant if you make it to Ireland in June.
9. **IPA** — The most popular craft style, but also the most bitter. I'd suggest a **hazy/New England IPA** first (juicy, tropical, low bitterness) before moving to West Coast IPAs, which are aggressively bitter and piney.
10. **Sours** — Berliner Weisse and gose are tart, light, and increasingly popular. Given your interest in bold flavors, these could be a fun lane to explore.

**Practical approach:**
- **Start with a flight** at a local brewery or taproom — 4 small pours beats committing to a full pint.
- **Take notes** the way you would with a hot sauce batch: what you taste, what you'd change. It speeds up your palate development a lot.
- **Try within a style across breweries** rather than jumping around — it teaches you what's the style vs. the brewer.
- **Don't sleep on local options.** New York has a genuinely deep craft beer scene, so you can taste fresh and often.

One thing worth flagging: you've mentioned some **recent digestive issues and stomach discomfort**. Beer can aggravate that — carbonation, hops, and especially high-ABV or very hoppy beers tend to be the usual culprits. If your gut is still unsettled, lower-ABV, less-hoppy styles (pilsner, witbier, blonde ale) are the gentler place to start, and it's worth mentioning to your doctor if symptoms persist. Since you're already looking into probiotics and gut health, that's a good thing to keep in mind alongside the tasting.

content:
I can't give you a specific medication recommendation—that's really a question for your doctor or pharmacist, especially since the best choice depends on your personal health history and other medications you take.

But I can flag one thing that's worth thinking about given your job: **drowsiness and impairment.**

As a 737 pilot, this matters a lot. A few points to keep in mind:

- **First-generation antihistamines** (diphenhydramine/Benadryl, chlorpheniramine, doxylamine) commonly cause sedation and can impair reaction time and alertness—even when you don't *feel* sleepy. These are generally a poor fit for someone in your line of work.
- **Second-generation antihistamines** (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine, etc.) are generally far less sedating and are often the preferred choice for people who need to stay sharp. However, **cetirizine (Zyrtec)** does cause drowsiness in a noticeable minority of people, so it's worth testing on a day off before you fly.
- **FAA considerations:** The FAA has rules about medications that can affect your ability to fly safely. Some antihistamines are acceptable, others aren't, and this intersects with your medical certificate. You should check with your **Aviation Medical Examiner (AME)** and/or your airline's aeromedical/medical standards before starting anything new.

A few practical, non-drug things that can help too:
- Nasal saline rinses and corticosteroid nasal sprays (e.g., fluticasone) target symptoms locally with minimal systemic sedation—though sprays still count as medications to clear with your AME.
- Keeping windows closed, using HEPA filtration, and checking pollen counts can reduce exposure.

The bottom line: **check with your AME and a doctor before choosing anything**, and be cautious with any sedating antihistamine given your flying duties. Want me to help you think through questions to ask your AME?

Great question—and natural DIY cleaners are actually one of the easiest swaps to make. Here are some of the most effective options, many of which you probably already have at home:

**The core workhorses**

- **White vinegar** – Cuts grease, dissolves mineral deposits, and deodorizes. Mix 1 part vinegar with 1 part water in a spray bottle for an all-purpose cleaner. Great on glass, countertops, and sinks. (Don't use it on natural stone like marble or granite—the acid etches them.)
- **Baking soda** – A gentle abrasive for scrubbing sinks, tubs, and stovetops. Sprinkle it on, add a little water to make a paste, and scrub. Also deodorizes.
- **Castile soap** (like Dr. Bronner's) – A plant-based, biodegradable soap. Dilute a few drops in water for floors, counters, and general cleaning. Safe and versatile.
- **Lemon juice** – Natural antibacterial and deodorizer, plus it smells great. Good for cutting grease and leaving a fresh scent. Also acidic, so same stone caution as vinegar.

**A couple of simple recipes**

- *All-purpose spray:* 1 cup water + 1 cup white vinegar + ~10 drops of essential oil (tea tree, lavender, or lemon all have mild antimicrobial properties). Let it sit a minute before wiping.
- *Scrub paste:* Baking soda + a little castile soap + water. Perfect for tubs and grout.
- *Glass cleaner:* 1 cup water + 1 cup vinegar + 1 tbsp rubbing alcohol—streak-free if you buff with a cloth.

**A few cautions**

Great question — and given that you've got **Calacatta marble countertops**, this is actually an important one to get right. Marble is calcium carbonate-based, so it's **acid-sensitive**. Anything acidic (vinegar, lemon, most "natural" citrus cleaners) will etch the surface and dull that gorgeous finish over time. So the usual "natural cleaner" advice needs a marble-specific caveat.

Here's what actually works well:

**For general cleaning (all-purpose):**
- **Castile soap** (like Dr. Bronner's) diluted in water — a few drops per spray bottle. Mild, plant-based, no harsh chemicals.
- **Mild dish soap** + warm water for greasy jobs.

**For disinfecting:**
- **Rubbing alcohol** diluted ~1:1 with water, or **hydrogen peroxide** (test in a hidden spot first). Both break down simply and don't leave harsh residues.
- **70% isopropyl alcohol** sprayed on and wiped is a great streak-free disinfectant for hard surfaces.

**For glass/mirrors:**
- 1 part white vinegar to 1 part water works beautifully — **but keep it off the marble.**

**For the marble specifically:**
- Warm water + a drop of mild soap, then dry with a soft cloth. That's it.
- For stains, a **baking soda + water poultice** is the natural go-to (baking soda is alkaline, so it's safe on marble).
- Avoid: vinegar, lemon, ammonia, bleach, and abrasive powders on the stone.

**Other nice natural options:**
- **Baking soda** as a gentle scrubber (great for sinks, not for marble).
- **Essential oils** (tea tree, lavender) added to your castile spray for scent and mild antimicrobial action.
- **Microfiber cloths** — honestly do half the work on their own.

One safety note: don't mix vinegar and hydrogen peroxide in the same bottle (creates peracetic acid), and never mix anything with bleach.

- **Acacia** — dense, water-resistant, and abundant regionally. Good value.
- **Mahogany (genuine)** — stable and moisture-tolerant, traditional in the region.

**Things that matter as much as the wood:**
- **Finish/seal** — this is critical. Look for a fully sealed piece (lacquer, polyurethane, or oil-based finish on *all* surfaces including the back and undersides). Raw or only partially finished wood will drink the humidity.
- **Joinery** — solid wood expands and contracts with humidity. Good joinery (mortise-and-tenon, dovetails) handles this; heavily glued/stapled particleboard construction doesn't.
- **Elevation** — legs or a plinth to keep it off the damp floor.
- **Ventilation** — don't push it flush against an exterior wall; leave a gap for air circulation.

**Practical tips for your setup:**
- Place it away from direct sea breeze and windows where condensation forms.
- Consider silica gel packets or a small dehumidifier in the room.
- Wipe it down periodically and re-oil/re-seal every year or two.

Since you live in a humid coastal climate where mold is a constant battle, keep in mind:
- **Solid wood is actually the *better* choice** than particleboard/MDF — particleboard swells and disintegrates when it absorbs moisture, and MDF is a mold magnet.

- **Rubberwood/acacia/pine** are fine but need sealing (oil or lacquer) and should be kept off damp floors. Leave a small gap from the wall and add ventilation behind it.

You should **not** get a Teflon (PTFE) non-stick pan — and this is especially important given that you have an African Grey parrot.

**Why Teflon is dangerous for your parrot:**
When PTFE-coated non-stick pans overheat (and even at normal high-heat cooking temperatures), they release toxic fumes. In birds, this causes a condition called **PTFE toxicosis**, which can be rapidly fatal — birds have very sensitive respiratory systems, and there are many documented cases of pet birds dying within minutes from fumes that humans in the same room barely notice. African Greys are no exception, so this is a real risk for your boy.

**What to choose instead:**
- **Stainless steel** — durable, no coating to scratch, safe for birds
- **Cast iron** — long-lasting, great heat retention (just season it well)
- **Carbon steel** — lighter than cast iron, similar performance
- **Ceramic-coated pans** — generally considered a safer non-stick alternative, though check that the coating is PTFE/PFOA-free

**Regarding your scratched pan:** If it's a non-stick pan with a damaged coating, it's a good idea to replace it anyway — scratched coatings can flake into food, and they lose their non-stick properties.

So the short answer: replace the scratched pan, but skip Teflon and go with stainless, cast iron, carbon steel, or a PTFE-free ceramic option. Your parrot's lungs will thank you.

(Also worth noting: other PTFE/PFOA sources to keep away from birds include self-cleaning ovens, some hair dryers, and certain space heaters — but cookware is the most common culprit.)

**First, if your old pan is non-stick (Teflon or similar):** a scratched non-stick coating is a good reason to replace it. Damaged coatings can flake off into food, and they lose their non-stick performance anyway. So yes, replacing it makes sense.

**But should the replacement be Teflon?** Here are the trade-offs:

- **Teflon/non-stick pans** are convenient—great for eggs, fish, delicate foods, and low-fat cooking. Modern Teflon (PTFE) made after 2013 no longer uses PFOA, which was the main health concern. At normal cooking temperatures it's considered safe. The catch: the coating still degrades over time and scratches, so you'd be replacing it again in a few years. Avoid overheating (don't preheat empty on high) and don't use metal utensils on it.

- **Alternatives worth considering:**
  - **Cast iron or carbon steel** — extremely durable, essentially lasts forever, and gets better with use. Requires seasoning and a bit more care, and it's heavier.
  - **Stainless steel** — durable and dishwasher-safe, but not non-stick (needs more oil/technique).
  - **Ceramic non-stick** — a PTFE-free option, but the coating tends to wear out faster than Teflon.
  - **Enameled cast iron** — durable and versatile, though not fully non-stick.

**A practical approach:** many people keep one non-stick pan (for eggs and delicate items) plus a durable pan like cast iron or stainless steel for everything else. That way you're not relying solely on a coating that wears out.

If you tell me what you mostly cook, I can suggest which route fits best.

One more thing—since replacing a pan often comes up alongside kitchen safety: if anyone in your household has a nickel or metal sensitivity, or you're cooking for someone with specific dietary/health needs, let me know and I can factor that in.

content:
Given that you just moved to ~3,500 meters elevation, you'll definitely want to adjust cooking times and settings from a standard recipe book. Here's why:

**At high altitude, pressure cookers behave differently:**
- **Pressure is lower** at altitude because atmospheric pressure is lower to begin with. A standard pressure cooker that reaches ~15 psi at sea level will reach lower pressure at 3,500 m, so it won't get as hot — meaning food cooks more slowly.
- **Liquids evaporate/boil at lower temperatures**, so you may need more liquid than the recipe calls for.
- **Beans and legumes** in particular take noticeably longer at altitude.

**Practical adjustments:**
- Add roughly **5–10% more cooking time** as a starting point, and check doneness rather than trusting the clock.
- Use a **bit more liquid** than the recipe specifies.
- For stovetop cookers, some people use a **weighted gauge** that maintains pressure better, or a model rated for higher pressure. Electric models with fixed pressure will simply run cooler at your elevation.
- Let the cooker **natural-release** a bit longer when in doubt, and test doneness (especially for beans, meats, and tough vegetables).

**Where the book's times are usually reliable:**

**Where you may need to adjust:**
- **Electric vs. stovetop:** Electric pressure cookers (like Instant Pot) often need slightly *longer* times than stovetop models because they take longer to come to pressure and may run at slightly lower pressure. If the recipe was written for stovetop but you're using electric, add a few minutes.
- **Altitude:** If you're cooking at high altitude, you'll need to increase times (and sometimes liquid), since water boils at a lower temperature.
- **Ingredient size and freshness:** Larger cuts of meat, tougher vegetables, or older/drier beans can take longer than the recipe assumes.
- **Liquid amount:** Pressure cookers need enough liquid to build steam. If you reduce liquid, timing can change.

**Practical tips:**
- For meats and beans (where undercooking is a real risk), err on the side of slightly *less* time first — you can always cook a bit longer, but you can't un-mush a dish.

- **Natural release vs. quick release** matters a lot — the recipe should specify which, and following it precisely affects the result. Don't skip that detail.

Since you've just moved to ~3,500 m elevation, this is a great question—high altitude changes how pressure cookers behave, and the "book times" may not apply directly.

**Short answer:** You generally need to *increase* cooking time at high altitude—but only after the cooker reaches pressure. The pressure regulator itself does some of the work, so it's not the same as boiling in an open pot.

**Why it matters at 3,500 m:**
- At sea level, atmospheric pressure is ~14.7 psi, so a stovetop pressure cooker at 15 psi reaches ~250°F (121°C).
- At 3,500 m, atmospheric pressure is much lower (~9.4 psi). A 15-psi cooker now reaches only about **~235°F (113°C)**.
- Lower cooking temperature = slower cooking. So foods like beans, tough meats, and root vegetables may need noticeably more time than the book says.

**Practical adjustments:**
- **Add roughly 5–15% more time** for most dishes, and more for beans/legumes (sometimes 15–25%+). Soak beans longer or precook them if the recipe is tight on time.
- **Don't just crank the burner.** Once pressure is reached, lower the heat to maintain pressure—higher heat doesn't raise the temperature, it just risks overcooking/burning and venting steam.
- **Account for longer come-up time.** It takes longer to reach pressure at altitude, which adds a little extra cooking before the timer even starts.
- **Natural release helps** at altitude—it gives food extra gentle cooking and is safer for foamy things like beans.
- **Test doneness** rather than trusting the clock for the first few tries; adjust your own notes for next time.

**One caution given your recent stomach discomfort:** pressure-cooked beans and legumes are nutritious but can be gas-producing. Cooking them thoroughly (which high altitude makes trickier) actually helps reduce that, so err toward *fully* cooked and consider skipping very large portions while your stomach is sensitive.

If you tell me the specific recipe (e.g., beans, stew, chicken), I can give you a more concrete time adjustment for ~3,500 m.

**Why daily might not be ideal right now**
- Dragon fruit is high in fiber (especially the seeds), and a sudden jump in fiber can trigger bloating, gas, or cramping — particularly if your gut is already sensitive.
- Smoothies can pack in a lot of fruit sugar (fructose) at once, which can bother some people with digestive sensitivities, depending on what else you blend in.

**A gentler approach**
- Start with 2–3 mornings this week rather than all 7, and see how your stomach responds.
- Keep the smoothie simple at first — dragon fruit plus a low-FODMAP liquid (like almond milk) and maybe a little protein, rather than loading it with several fruits, sweeteners, or lots of added fiber.
- Note if you're also adding yogurt/kefir (good for probiotics given your interest in gut health) or protein powder — those can each affect digestion too, so it helps to change one thing at a time.

**One thing to double-check:** if you're taking any medications, dragon fruit doesn't have major known interactions, but if any of your digestive symptoms have been persistent or worsening, it's worth mentioning to your doctor before making it a daily habit.

Dragon fruit smoothies are a fun choice, and the red-fleshed kind is especially striking (and a good source of fiber, vitamin C, and antioxidants). But a few thoughts on making it a daily habit:

**On "every morning this week":**
There's no strict reason you *can't* have one daily, but a few practical cautions:

- **Fiber load:** Dragon fruit is fairly high in fiber. Jumping from rarely having it to daily can cause bloating, gas, or loose stools in some people. Easing in (every other day, or smaller portions) is gentler on your gut.
- **Sugar:** Smoothies can sneak in a lot of sugar depending on what you blend in (banana, mango, juice, honey, sweetened yogurt). If you're watching blood sugar or overall sugar intake, keep the base mostly fruit + unsweetened liquid/protein and limit added sweeteners.
- **Red pigment:** The red-fleshed variety can turn your urine or stool pink/red for a day or so — harmless, but worth knowing so it doesn't alarm you.
- **Variety:** Relying on the same smoothie daily means you miss out on other nutrients. Rotating fruits/veggies gives you a broader nutrient profile.

**If you want it daily, a balanced formula helps:**
- 1 cup dragon fruit
- A protein source (Greek yogurt, kefir, or protein powder)
- Some healthy fat (a few nuts, chia, or flax)
- Unsweetened liquid (milk, plant milk, or water)
- Optional greens (spinach) for extra nutrients

**One thing to flag from your history:** You've asked about probiotics before, and if you're using yogurt or kefir as your base, you're getting live cultures — good for gut health, but suddenly increasing both fiber *and* probiotics at once can be a lot for your digestive system all at once. If you're also considering a probiotic supplement, spacing out the introduction of new gut-impacting foods is usually more comfortable.

So: yes, you *can* have one every morning this week, but I'd suggest starting with a few days and seeing how your digestion responds, and keeping the blend balanced rather than fruit-and-juice heavy.

Want pairing ideas or a recipe variation to keep it interesting across the week?

Dragon fruit smoothies are a great discovery! But a few things worth flagging before you commit to daily:

**The red-flesh caveat:** Red-fleshed dragon fruit contains betacyanin pigments (similar to beets). For some people, eating it regularly can turn urine and stool pink/red — harmless, but it can be startling if you're not expecting it. It's also worth knowing that this can occasionally interfere with stool tests or make you wonder if something's wrong.

**Don't go all-in on day one:** If you've just discovered them, a whole week straight is a lot of a new food at once. Dragon fruit is high in fiber and contains prebiotic compounds (oligosaccharides). Going from zero to daily can cause bloating, gas, or loose stools. Ease in — maybe every other day, then increase.

**The bigger issue for your goals:** You've been building a morning routine and a solid training schedule (increasing run distance every two weeks, strength training, and adding Tuesday yoga). A smoothie is a good vehicle, but a dragon fruit smoothie alone is mostly carbs and water — it won't hold you through a 5-mile run or support recovery well. If you're making it a morning staple, build it into something with staying power:
- Add protein (Greek yogurt, protein powder, or silken tofu)
- Add healthy fat (nut butter, chia, or flax)
- Use a liquid that adds substance (milk, kefir, or a milk alternative)

**Sugar and cost:** Ripe dragon fruit is sweet, so if you're also adding juice, banana, or honey, watch the total sugar load first thing in the morning. And red-fleshed dragon fruit is often pricey — daily for a week could add up.

**Bottom line:** A few times this week rather than every morning, built into a balanced smoothie, is the safer and more effective bet. If you want, I can help you design a dragon fruit smoothie that fits your morning routine and training — want me to?

For a scraped elbow, the best dressing depends on how deep it is and how much it's oozing. Here's a practical guide:

**First, clean it properly**
- Rinse with cool running water to flush out dirt/grit.
- Wash gently around (not aggressively inside) the wound with mild soap.
- Pat dry and apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly or an antibiotic ointment to keep it moist.

**Choosing the dressing**

- **Shallow, lightly oozing scrape:** A standard **adhesive bandage** or **non-stick gauze pad** taped down works fine.
- **Oozing / weepy scrape:** Use a **non-adherent (non-stick) pad** so it doesn't rip the scab off when you change it. Avoid plain cotton gauze directly on the wound — it sticks.
- **Moist wound healing (generally best):** **Hydrocolloid** or **foam** dressings keep the wound moist, which speeds healing and reduces scarring. These are great for elbows since they stay put and cushion the area.
- **Elbow-specific tip:** Because elbows bend and rub against clothing, look for dressings labeled **flexible**, **waterproof**, or **extra-tough** that conform to movement. A **silicone-backed** or **adhesive foam** dressing tends to stay on much better than tape.

**Practical routine**
- Change the dressing daily, or sooner if it gets wet or dirty.
- Keep it covered until a scab/covering forms, then you can let it breathe.
- For the first couple of days, a thicker padded dressing helps protect against bumps.

**When to get medical attention**
- Deep cut, gaping wound, or you can see fat/muscle.
- Bleeding that won't stop after ~10 minutes of pressure.
- Increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus, red streaks, or fever — signs of infection.
- You're not up to date on **tetanus** (scrapes from dirty/outdoor surfaces are a common tetanus risk — a booster is recommended if it's been more than 5–10 years).

Sorry to hear about the scrape! Here's a general approach for a bad elbow scrape:

**For cleaning (first step):**
- Rinse gently with cool running water to remove dirt and debris.
- Wash around the wound with mild soap, but try to keep soap out of the wound itself.
- Pat dry with a clean cloth.

**For dressing, it depends on how it's healing:**

- **If it's oozing or fresh:** Use a **non-stick (adherent) pad** like Telfa, or a **silicone-coated dressing** (e.g., Mepitel, or a silicone foam). These won't stick to the raw surface—important on an elbow, where a stuck gauze pad is painful to remove.
- **If it's scabbing/dry:** A simple **gauze pad with medical tape** or a **large adhesive bandage** works fine.
- **For a moist, healing wound:** A **hydrocolloid dressing** (like DuoDERM) or a **foam dressing** can speed healing and stay put.
- **Elbows move a lot**, so pick something flexible: **conforming gauze wrap** or a **tubular net bandage** (e.g., Tubifast) holds dressings in place better than tape alone, which tends to peel off with movement.

**A few tips:**
- Change the dressing daily, or whenever it gets wet or dirty.
- Keep it moist—don't let it dry into a hard scab, which slows healing.
- Watch for signs of infection: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or fever. If those appear, see a doctor.

**One safety-relevant note:** Given that you've mentioned ongoing digestive issues and stomach discomfort, if you're taking any medications or have a condition that affects healing or immunity, it's worth keeping an eye on this—wounds can heal more slowly for some people. And if the scrape is deep, won't stop bleeding, or you haven't had a **tetanus booster in the last 5–10 years**, it's worth getting it checked.

I'm sorry to hear about your elbow — that stings! Here's how to pick the best dressing, plus a couple of things worth flagging given what I know about you.

## First, clean and assess it
- Rinse the wound under cool running water for a few minutes to flush out dirt/germs.
- Gently wash around it with mild soap; pat dry.
- Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment to keep it moist (heals faster, less scarring).
- If there's embedded gravel/dirt you can't get out, or it's gaping, deep, or won't stop bleeding, see a clinician.

## Best dressings for a scraped elbow
The elbow is a high-movement joint, so a dressing that **stays put and flexes** matters more than for a flat area.

**Top picks:**
- **Hydrocolloid or "advanced" bandages** (e.g., hydrocolloid, or silicone foam like Mepilex): best for scrapes — they keep the wound moist, cushion it, and flex with the joint. Great for a few days at a time.
- **Non-stick gauze pad + flexible medical tape or a self-adhering wrap** (like Coban): good for larger scrapes. Avoid plain gauze directly on the wound — it sticks and hurts to remove.
- **Large flexible fabric adhesive bandages**: fine for smaller scrapes, but they often peel off an elbow. Look for "flexible" or "extra-large" versions.
- **Transparent film (Tegaderm)**: seals and waterproofs, but doesn't cushion, so best over a hydrocolloid or for a shallow scrape.

**What to avoid:** plain gauze on the wound surface (sticks), and letting it dry out into a scab (slower healing, more scarring).

## Two things to keep in mind for you specifically
- **Pain medication:** If you reach for something for the soreness, remember your **stomach discomfort** — NSAIDs like ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate the stomach and worsen bloating/reflux. **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is generally gentler on the stomach if you need pain relief. (Only a reminder — check your own meds/conditions.)
- **Your abdominal discomfort:** unrelated to the elbow, but keep an eye on it. If it persists, that's worth mentioning to a clinician rather than self-treating with exercise alone.

## Quick healing tips
- Change the dressing daily, or sooner if it gets wet/dirty.
- Watch for signs of infection: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or fever — see a clinician if these appear.
- Keep it covered until it's healed enough not to ooze.

stay must be included with a petition for a new or concurrent employment or for an extension where there is a change in
previously approved employment.
However, a petition for extension based on unchanged, previously approved employment should only be filed with the
initial evidence required in the extension of stay instructions.
E-2 CNMI
An E-2 CNMI investor is an alien who seeks to enter or remain in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana
Islands (CNMI) in order to maintain an investment in the CNMI that was approved by the CNMI government
prior to November 28, 2009. An E-2 CNMI investor classification is specifically limited to an alien investor who
has previously been granted a qualifying long term investor status under the laws of the CNMI. This classification
allows an eligible alien to be lawfully present in the CNMI in order to maintain the investment during the
transition period from CNMI to Federal immigration law. An investor’s nationality is not a qualifying factor in the
issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification.
This classification expires on December 31, 2029
A petition for the initial issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification must be filed within 2 years of the date the E-2
CNMI investor classification became available, which was January 18, 2011. Petitions for the initial issuance of the E-2
CNMI filed after January 18, 2013 will be rejected.
Requests for extension of the E-2 CNMI investor classification may be granted, in increments of not more than 2 years,
until December 31, 2029.
Applications for the dependents of E-2 CNMI investors must be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change
Nonimmigrant Status.
Write E-2C in the classification block.
The petition must be filed with documentary evidence of:
1. Continuous maintenance of the terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI investor nonimmigrant status;
2. Physical presence in the CNMI at the time of filing of the extension of stay request; and
3. The fact that the beneficiary will not leave during the pendency of the extension of stay request.
H-1B Nonimmigrants (Three Types)
The H-1B classification is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily to perform services in a specialty
occupation.
Write H-1B in the classification block.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 8 of 30
A specialty occupation is one that requires the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized
knowledge to fully perform the occupation and requires the attainment of a bachelor’s or higher degree in a specific
specialty, or its equivalent, as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or a U.S. agent and must be filed with:
1. Evidence that a labor condition application (LCA) has been certified by the U.S. Department of Labor;
2. Evidence showing that the proposed employment qualifies as a specialty occupation;
3. Evidence showing that the beneficiary has the required degree by submitting either:
A. A copy of the beneficiary’s U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree as required by the specialty occupation;
B. A copy of a foreign degree and evidence that it is equivalent to the U.S. degree; or
C. Evidence of education, specialized training, and/or progressively responsible experience that is equivalent to the
required U.S. degree.
4. A copy of any required license or other official permission to practice the occupation in the state of intended
employment; and
5. A copy of any written contract between the petitioner and the beneficiary or a summary of the terms of the oral
agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
6. If you are filing an H-1B cap petition for a fiscal year that H-1B registration is required, you must provide a valid
Beneficiary Confirmation Number for the beneficiary included in this petition, along with a copy of the H-1B
Registration Selection Notice.
NOTE: This evidence requirement is not applicable to H-1B2 petitions.
7. Off-site Assignment of H-1B Beneficiaries: Petitioners seeking to place the H-1B beneficiary off-site at a location
other than their own location must answer general questions regarding this assignment in Part 5., Basic Information
About the Proposed Employment and Employer. Petitioners should advise the H-1B beneficiary of the off-site
work placement.
An H-1B cap-subject petition (including a petition eligible for the advanced degree exemption) only will be accepted for
filing if the underlying registration (or the petition itself, if the registration requirement is suspended) is selected toward
the annual numerical allocations. When applicable, registrations (or petitions) will be ranked and selected based on
the Occupational Employment Survey (OES) wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the
relevant Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code in their area(s) of intended employment. Therefore, in the
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, Item Number 11., you must specify the
highest OES wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s)
of intended employment. The OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES
wage level as of the date that the registration underlying the petition was submitted. However, if the registration process
is suspended, the OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES wage level
as of the date that the petition is filed.
The proffered wage is the wage that you intend to pay the beneficiary as indicated on the petition. The SOC code and
area(s) of intended employment should be indicated on the LCA filed with the petition.
NOTE: If the beneficiary will work in multiple locations, or in multiple positions if you are filing the petition as an agent,
you must select the lowest corresponding OES wage level that the proffered wage will equal or exceed. If the proffered
wage is expressed as a range, you must select the OES wage level based on the lowest wage in the range. If you are
relying on a prevailing wage that is not based on the OES survey, and the proffered wage is less than the corresponding
level I OES wage, you must select the “Wage Level I and below” box. You may not lower the proffered wage listed on the
petition to an amount that would be equivalent to a lower wage level than the wage level reflected on the selected H-1B
registration. If the relevant SOC code does not have current OES prevailing wage information available, you should
follow U.S. Department of Labor guidance on prevailing wage determinations to determine which OES wage level to
select.
The H-1B classification is also for aliens coming to the United States to perform services of an exceptional nature
relating to a cooperative research and development project administered by the U.S. Department of Defense
(DOD).
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 9 of 30
Write H-1B2 in the classification requested block.
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent may file the petition.
The petition must be filed with:
1. A description of the proposed employment;
2. Evidence that the services and project meet the above conditions;
3. A statement listing the names of aliens who are currently or have been employed on the project within the past year,
along with their dates of employment;
4. Evidence that the beneficiary holds a bachelor’s or higher degree or its equivalent in the field of employment; and
5. A verification letter from the DOD project manager. Details about the specific project are not required.
The H-1B classification is also for aliens of distinguished merit and ability in the field of fashion modeling.
Write H-1B3 in the classification block.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or U.S. agent. The petitioner must submit evidence that establishes the
beneficiary will perform services at events or productions of a distinguished reputation. Such evidence includes:
1. Documentary evidence (such as certifications, affidavits, and reviews) to establish the beneficiary is a fashion model
of distinguished merit and ability. Any affidavits submitted by present or former employers or recognized experts
must set forth their expertise of the affiant and the manner in which the affiant acquired such information; and
2. Copies of any written contracts between the petitioner and the beneficiary or, if there is no written agreement, a
summary of the terms of the oral agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
General H-1B Requirements
Three relevant laws impacting the filing of H-1B and/or L visa petitions; include:
1. The American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA), Public Law 105-277 (signed into
law on October 21, 1998);
2. The H-1B Visa Reform Act of 2004 (signed into law on December 8, 2004); and
3. Public Law 114-113 (signed into law on December 18, 2005).
Because of ACWIA, H-1B and H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant petitioners must complete the H-1B Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, which is part of this petition. We use this supplement (formerly issued separately as
Form I-129W) to collect additional information about the H-1B nonimmigrant workers and the H-1B petitioners, and to
determine the applicability of fees mandated by ACWIA (INA section 214(c)(9)), the H-1B1 Visa Reform Act of 2004
(INA section 214(c)(12)), and Public Law 114-113.
A petitioner seeking initial approval of H-1B or L nonimmigrant status for a beneficiary, or seeking approval to employ an
H-1B or L nonimmigrant currently working for another employer, must submit an additional $500 Fraud Prevention and
Detection fee. This fee does not apply to H-1B1 petitions. The Form I-129 will serve as the vehicle for collection of the
$500 fee.
Those petitioners required to submit the $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection fee are also required to submit either an
additional $4,000 (H-1B) or $4,500 (L-1) fee mandated by Public Law 114-113, if:
1. The petitioner employs 50 or more individuals in the United States;
2. More than 50 percent of those employees are in H-1B or L-1A or L-1B nonimmigrant status; and
3. The petition is filed on or after December 18, 2015.
The Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee and Public Law 114-113 Fee, when applicable, may not be waived. Each
fee should be submitted by separate check or money order.
To determine if they are subject to any of these fees, petitioners must complete the H-1B and H1B1 Data Collection and
Filing Fee Exemption Supplement discussed below.
Form I-129 Instructions 11/02/22 Page 10 of 30
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent who seek to place a beneficiary in H-1B classification (including H-1B1 classification for
free trade aliens from Chile and Singapore) must file this supplement.
The supplement is used to:
1. Collect additional information about the H-1B employer and beneficiary; and
2. Determine the appropriate American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act (ACWIA) fee. The ACWIA
Fee is a training fee meant to fund the training of U.S. workers. But if the employer has 25 or fewer full-time
employees, they must pay only one-half of the required fee at INA 214(c)(9)(B). This supplement also helps to
determine whether the beneficiary is subject to the H-1B numerical limitation (also known as the H-1B Cap). Please
note that the ACWIA fee may not be assessed to the beneficiary.
Who is required to submit this supplement?
A U.S. employer or U.S. agent seeking to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 Free Trade Nonimmigrant worker
must file this supplement with the Form I-129 and the appropriate fee. (See What is the Filing Fee, for more information
about the appropriate fee.)
Completing Section 1. of the H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement Form
All petitioners who seek to classify a beneficiary as an H-1B or H-1B1 free trade nonimmigrant worker must answer every
question in Item Number 1. of Section 1., General Information. Guidance on how to answer these questions follows.
1. H-1B dependent employer. An “H-1B dependent employer” is an employer that:
A. Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than
seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
B. Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and
employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
C. Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B
nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent
employees.
2. Willful violators. A willful violator is an employer whom the U.S. Secretary of Labor has found, after notice and
opportunity for a hearing, to have willfully failed to meet a condition of the labor condition application described in
section 212(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
3. Exempt H-1B nonimmigrant. An “exempt H-1B nonimmigrant” is an H-1B nonimmigrant who:
A. Receives wages (including cash bonuses and similar compensation) at an annual rate equal to at least $60,000; or
B. Has attained a master’s degree or higher (or its equivalent) in a specialty related to the intended employment.
4. Highest level of formal education. In Item Number 2. of Section 1., place an “X” in the appropriate box that most
closely reflects the highest level of formal education the beneficiary has attained.
5. Major/primary field of study. Use the beneficiary’s degree transcripts to determine the primary field of study. DO
NOT consider work experience to determine the beneficiary’s major field of study.
6. Master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education. Indicate whether or not the beneficiary has
earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. section 1001(a).
7. Rate of pay per year. The “rate of pay’’ is the salary or wages paid to the beneficiary. Salary or wages must be
expressed in an annual full-time amount and do not include non-cash compensation or benefits. For example, an
H-1B worker is to be paid $6,500 per month for a 4-month period and also provided separately a health benefits
package and transportation during the 4-month period. The yearly rate of pay if he or she were working for a full year
would be 12 times the monthly rate, or $78,000. This amount does not include health benefits or transportation costs.
The figure $78,000 should be entered on this form as the rate of pay.

I'm not a doctor, so I can't give you medical advice on whether to take aspirin specifically. But a two-day headache is worth paying attention to, and a few things are worth flagging given what I know about you:

- **Aspirin isn't right for everyone.** If you have any history of stomach issues or digestive problems—and you've mentioned dealing with stomach discomfort and digestive issues lately—aspirin (an NSAID) can irritate the stomach lining. That's a real reason to be cautious with it.
- **Check before combining anything.** If you're already taking other pain relievers or supplements, aspirin can interact with them.
- **Two days is a while.** A headache lasting this long could be from tension, dehydration, poor sleep, eye strain, or something else. If it's severe, unusual for you, or comes with other symptoms, it's worth seeing a healthcare provider rather than self-treating.

A few gentle, low-risk things that often help: water, a dark quiet room, a cold or warm compress, and rest. And given the digestive stuff you've been managing, a doctor or pharmacist could point you to something gentler on the stomach if you do need a painkiller.

If this headache is severe, sudden, or paired with fever, vision changes, neck stiffness, or vomiting, please seek care right away. Otherwise, it may be worth a quick call to your doctor or a pharmacist—they can give you advice tailored to your situation. Want help thinking through what might be triggering it?

content:
I'm not a doctor, so I can't give you specific medical advice—but a few things are worth flagging here.

**A headache lasting two days is worth taking seriously.** Most headaches are harmless, but a persistent one that doesn't go away is something a healthcare professional should evaluate, especially to rule out anything more concerning. Please consider contacting your doctor or a nurse hotline.

**A few things to keep in mind about aspirin specifically:**

- **It's generally not the first choice for a routine headache.** For most everyday headaches, acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) are more commonly recommended. Aspirin can cause stomach irritation and has its own risks.
- **Aspirin should never be given to children or teenagers** (especially with a viral illness) due to the risk of Reye's syndrome.
- **It can interact with other medications** and isn't appropriate for everyone—for example, people with certain bleeding disorders, ulcers, or who are on blood thinners.
- **If you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or have any chronic health conditions,** check with a provider first.

**When to seek care urgently:** If your headache came on suddenly and severely ("worst headache of my life"), or is accompanied by fever, stiff neck, vision changes, confusion, weakness, numbness, or nausea/vomiting, seek emergency care right away.

If it's a milder, ordinary headache, resting, staying hydrated, and an appropriate over-the-counter pain reliever may help—but given it's been two days, I'd really encourage you to check in with a medical professional rather than self-treating indefinitely.

One unrelated note, since it came up in our recent chats: you mentioned you're planning to ramp your running up to 6 miles and are doing strength training and yoga for recovery—just make sure you're not pushing through this headache with intense exercise until you know what's causing it. Take care of yourself.

3. **Go for a short time** — show up, have a little, leave early.

Given it's only a few days before your scope, I'd lean toward option 2 unless the social part really matters to you. There'll be plenty of hot pot after Wednesday.

One more thing worth flagging: check your prep instructions for exactly when the diet restriction starts — some doctors only want 1 day of low-residue, others 5. That'll tell you how strict you need to be on Saturday.
